abbagliamento.t: Built on abbagliare (to dazzle) with the noun ending -mento: the dazzling itself, a sudden glare that blinds for a moment.

abbagliante.t: The present participle of abbagliare (to dazzle): the dazzling light, which is why the high beam carries this name.

abbagliati.t: The past participle of abbagliare (to dazzle): dazzled, blinded for a moment by a strong light.

abbigliamento.t: Borrowed from the French habillement, from habiller (to dress): what a person is dressed in, clothing or gear.

abbinato.t: From a derivative of the Latin bini (two by two, a pair), the same word behind the English "binary": to match or pair two things.

abilita.t: Built on abilità (ability, skill): abilitare is to make someone capable, and so to qualify them for a profession or a task.

abilitante.t: Built on abilità (ability, skill): abilitare is to make someone capable, and so to qualify them for a profession or a task.

abilitato.t: Built on abilità (ability, skill): abilitare is to make someone capable, and so to qualify them for a profession or a task.

abitacolo.t: From the Late Latin habitaculum (a dwelling), from habitare (to reside, to inhabit): the part of the vehicle where the people sit.

abusivamente.t: Not "abusively": abusivamente means without authorization or unlawfully, as in something done without the required permit. It comes from abusivo, from Latin abusivus, built on abusus, a misuse; Italian applies the idea of misuse to acting without permission, while English "abuse" came to mean harsh treatment or insulting language.

accensione.t: From accendere (to switch on, to light): the switching on, and so the ignition of an engine.

accertamento.t: From accertare, built from a- and certo (certain): the act of making certain, a check or official verification.

accertandosi.t: Built from a- and certo (certain): accertare is to make sure of something or to verify it, and accertarsi is to make sure.

accertarci.t: Built from a- and certo (certain): accertare is to make sure of something or to verify it, and accertarsi is to make sure.

accertare.t: Built from a- and certo (certain): accertare is to make sure of something or to verify it, and accertarsi is to make sure.

accertarsi.t: Built from a- and certo (certain): accertare is to make sure of something or to verify it, and accertarsi is to make sure.

accertato.t: Built from a- and certo (certain): accertare is to make sure of something or to verify it, and accertarsi is to make sure.

accerti.t: Built from a- and certo (certain): accertare is to make sure of something or to verify it, and accertarsi is to make sure.

accettazione.t: Related to the English "acceptance", both from the Latin acceptare: accettazione is also the admissions or check-in desk, where people are received as they arrive.

acciaio.t: From the Late Latin aciarium, derived from acies (a sharp point): steel.

accinge.t: From accingersi, to gird oneself, as in the English "cinch": to get ready to do something, so to be about to do it.

accodarsi.t: From a- and coda (tail, queue): to get in line at the tail of someone else.

accogliere.t: From a Latin compound of ad- and colligere (to gather), the source of cogliere: to take in, so to receive, hold or accept.

accorgimenti.t: From accorgersi (to notice, to become aware): foresight, and the shrewd measures it suggests, such as precautions.

accortezza.t: From accorto (alert, shrewd), the participle of accorgersi (to notice): the quality of being alert, care or caution.

accostarci.t: From a- and costa (side, rib, as in "coast"): to bring alongside, so to pull over toward the edge.

accostare.t: From a- and costa (side, rib, as in "coast"): to bring alongside, so to pull over toward the edge.

accostarsi.t: From a- and costa (side, rib, as in "coast"): to bring alongside, so to pull over toward the edge.

accusa.t: Besides "accuses", said of a person accusa can mean shows or reports a symptom, as in accusa stanchezza, shows tiredness.

acquaragia.t: From acqua (water) and ragia (pine resin): turpentine.

adeguare.t: From the Latin adaequare, built on aequare (to make equal): adeguare is to make something match a need, to adjust or adapt it.

aderenza.t: Related to the English "adherence" and "adhesion", from the Latin for sticking to: for a vehicle, aderenza is the grip of the tires on the road.

adibito.t: From the Latin adhibere (to apply, to put to use): something put to a given use, designated for it.

adoperarsi.t: From adoperare (to use, to put to work), built on operare: adoperarsi is to set oneself to work, to do all one can.

affaticamento.t: Built on fatica (effort, weariness), like the English "fatigue": the state of being worn out.

affaticati.t: Built on fatica (effort, weariness), like the English "fatigue": the state of being worn out.

affianca.t: From a- and fianco (side, like the English "flank"): to come up at someone's side.

affiancano.t: From a- and fianco (side, like the English "flank"): to come up at someone's side.

affiancati.t: From a- and fianco (side, like the English "flank"): to come up at someone's side.

affidamento.t: From the medieval Latin affidamentum, an entrusting: fare affidamento su means to rely or count on someone or something.

affinché.t: From a fine che, literally "to the end that": so that, in order that.

afflusso.t: From the medieval Latin affluxus, from affluere (to flow toward): the flowing of something toward a place, a flow or supply.

affrettato.t: Built on fretta (hurry, haste): affrettare is to hurry, and affrettato is hurried or rushed.

affretti.t: Built on fretta (hurry, haste): affrettare is to hurry, and affrettato is hurried or rushed.

affrontare.t: From a Latin verb built on frons (forehead, front): to face something head on, to meet or tackle it.

agendo.t: From the Latin agere (to drive forward, to do), through the French agir, the root of the English "agent": to act, to work.

agevolare.t: Built on agevole (easy), which probably comes from agio (ease), the same source as the English "ease": to make easier.

agevolmente.t: From agevole (easy), which probably comes from agio (ease), the same source as the English "ease": easily, without effort.

agganciare.t: Built on gancio (hook): to hook one thing onto another, to hitch or couple.

agganciato.t: Built on gancio (hook): to hook one thing onto another, to hitch or couple.

aggancio.t: Built on gancio (hook): the hooking, or a part catching on something.

aggiornare.t: From a- and giorno (day): to update, to bring something up to date.

aggirare.t: From a- and giro (turn, circle, as in "gyrate"): to go around something.

agire.t: From the Latin agere (to drive forward, to do), through the French agir, the root of the English "agent": to act, to work.

agisce.t: From the Latin agere (to drive forward, to do), through the French agir, the root of the English "agent": to act, to work.

alettature.t: Related to aletta, a small ala (wing) that also means a fin: alettatura is a whole set of fins taken together.

alianti.t: Picture wings (ali) spread wide and no engine: an aliante is a glider.

alimentazione.t: Related to the English "aliment" and "alimentary", from the Latin alimentum, nourishment: alimentazione is feeding, and in a vehicle the supply of fuel or power to the engine.

allaccia.t: Built on laccio (lace, cord), like the English "lace": to fasten or buckle.

allacciamento.t: From allacciare (to fasten), built on laccio (lace, cord): a connection or hookup.

allacciare.t: Built on laccio (lace, cord), like the English "lace": to fasten or buckle.

allacciato.t: Built on laccio (lace, cord), like the English "lace": to fasten or buckle.

allaccino.t: Built on laccio (lace, cord), like the English "lace": to fasten or buckle.

allagamento.t: Built on lago (lake): for water to cover an area as if it were a lake, to flood.

allagarsi.t: Built on lago (lake): for water to cover an area as if it were a lake, to flood.

allargamento.t: Built on largo, which mainly means wide: allargare is to widen, and allargamento is a widening.

allarghi.t: Built on largo, which mainly means wide: allargare is to widen, and allargamento is a widening.

alleggerisce.t: Built on leggero (light in weight): to make lighter, to ease.

allenare.t: Built on lena (energy, vigor): to build up someone's energy, which is to train or coach.

allentare.t: Built on lento, which means slack as well as slow: to make slack, to loosen.

alloggiare.t: Related to the English "lodge": alloggiare is to lodge or stay, and alloggio is lodging.

alloggio.t: Related to the English "lodge": alloggiare is to lodge or stay, and alloggio is lodging.

allontana.t: Built on lontano (far): to move away, literally to make far.

allontanare.t: Built on lontano (far): to move away, literally to make far.

allontanarsi.t: Built on lontano (far): to move away, literally to make far.

allorché.t: From allora and che joined into one word: a literary word meaning when, used in place of quando.

altrui.t: From a Latin form of alter (other): belonging to other people, as in la sicurezza altrui, the safety of others.

ammontare.t: From a- and monte (mountain): what things pile up to, like the English "amount", which comes from the same root.

ammortizzatori.t: From ammortizzare, built on morte (death): to make dead. The English "amortize" has the same origin, and to amortize a debt is to make it dead, killing it off payment by payment. An ammortizzatore does the same to the jolts of the road: it makes them die away.

anabbagliante.t: From an- (not, as in "anonymous") and abbagliante (dazzling): the beam that does not dazzle, the low beam.

andatura.t: From andare (to go): the way something goes, its pace or gait.

anello.t: From the Latin anellus, a little ring, related to the English "annular": a ring.

animosamente.t: Related to the English "animosity", from the Latin animosus, spirited: animosamente means heatedly or with hostility, and also boldly, with courage.

anticipo.t: Not "anticipate" in the sense of expect: anticipare usually means to bring something forward or do it earlier, and in anticipo means ahead of time. Both come from Latin anticipare, to take beforehand, from ante (before) and capere (to take); English first used "anticipate" for causing something to happen sooner and only later for expecting it, while Italian kept the older sense.

antifurto.t: From anti- (against) and furto (theft, related to the English "furtive"): a device against theft.

antistante.t: From the Latin antistare, to stand before: something that stands in front of something else.

appannamento.t: Built on panno (cloth): a glass covered as if by a veil of cloth, fogged or misted up.

apparecchi.t: Related to the English "apparatus", from the Latin apparare (to prepare): a device or piece of equipment.

apparecchio.t: Related to the English "apparatus", from the Latin apparare (to prepare): a device or piece of equipment.

appendice.t: The same word as the English "appendix", from the Latin appendix, something attached: here appendice means an add-on, a part attached to something else.

appoggio.t: From appoggiare (to lean on or rest on), which comes from the Latin podium, also the source of the English "podium": a support or footing.

apporre.t: From the Latin apponere (to place on), as in the English "apposition": apporre is to affix, and apposto is affixed.

appositamente.t: Not "opposite": appositamente means on purpose or specially, from apposito, suitable or special. Apposito comes from Latin appositus, placed near, which also gave the rare English "apposite", fitting; "opposite" comes from a different Latin word, oppositus, set against.

apposito.t: Not "opposite": apposito means suitable or special, like the rare English "apposite", both from the Latin appositus. Appositus means placed near, from ad, to, and ponere, to put, while "opposite" comes from oppositus, placed against, so the two differ only in the prefix.

apposto.t: From the Latin apponere (to place on), as in the English "apposition": apporre is to affix, and apposto is affixed.

approfittare.t: From a- and profitto (profit): to draw profit from something, to take advantage of it.

approssima.t: Related to the English "approximate", both from the Latin approximare, to come near: approssimarsi means to approach or draw near.

approssimarsi.t: Related to the English "approximate", both from the Latin approximare, to come near: approssimarsi means to approach or draw near.

arco.t: The same word as the English "arc", both from the Latin arcus: nell'arco delle ventiquattro ore treats the day as one sweep, meaning over its whole span.

argine.t: From the Latin agger, through a popular form arger: an embankment that holds a river in when it floods.

arreca.t: From a- and recare (to bring): to bring on, to cause, usually harm or trouble.

arrecare.t: From a- and recare (to bring): to bring on, to cause, usually harm or trouble.

arrecati.t: From a- and recare (to bring): to bring on, to cause, usually harm or trouble.

arrestano.t: Related to the English "arrest", whose first sense was to cause to stop: arrestare means to stop, and arrestarsi is to come to a halt.

arrestarci.t: Related to the English "arrest", whose first sense was to cause to stop: arrestare means to stop, and arrestarsi is to come to a halt.

arrestare.t: Related to the English "arrest", whose first sense was to cause to stop: arrestare means to stop, and arrestarsi is to come to a halt.

arrestato.t: Related to the English "arrest", whose first sense was to cause to stop: arrestare means to stop, and arrestarsi is to come to a halt.

arresto.t: Related to the English "arrest", whose first sense was to cause to stop: arrestare means to stop, and arrestarsi is to come to a halt.

arrotolatore.t: Built on rotolo (a roll): the device that rolls the belt back up.

articolazioni.t: Related to the English "articulation", from Latin articulus, a small joint. An articulated bus bends at a joint, and articolazioni are the joints of the body.

artigianale.t: Built on artigiano (artisan): made by hand rather than in a factory.

arto.t: From the Latin artus (joint, limb), related to "article" and "articulation": an arm or a leg.

asciutto.t: From the Latin exsuctus (sucked out), as in "suction": with the moisture drawn out, dry.

asini.t: From asino, from the Latin asinus (donkey), the source of the English "asinine".

asl.t: Short for Azienda Sanitaria Locale, the local health authority.

asperità.t: Related to the English "asperity" (roughness): both come from the Latin asper, rough.

asse.t: From the Latin axis. In Italian asse is also the axis of geometry and physics, but here it is the axle, the rod a pair of wheels turns on.

assetto.t: Sounds like "a set": the assetto of a vehicle is how it is set on its wheels, its balance and trim.

assicurarsi.t: From sicuro (sure, secure), through a Latin form built on securus: to make sure, to make secure, or to insure.

assicurati.t: From sicuro (sure, secure), through a Latin form built on securus: to make sure, to make secure, or to insure.

assicurativa.t: From assicurare (to make secure, to insure): assicurativo describes anything to do with an insurance policy.

assicurazione.t: From assicurare (to make secure, to insure): assicurativo describes anything to do with an insurance policy.

assimilato.t: Related to the English "assimilate", both from the Latin assimilare, to make like: here assimilato means treated as the same as something else, counted as equal to it.

assoggettato.t: From a- and soggetto (subject): made subject to, as in the English "subjected".

assolata.t: From sole, the sun: an assolata road is one exposed to the full sun.

assume.t: Like "assume" in part, but here assumere means to take in or ingest a substance, and it also means to hire.

assunto.t: Like "assume" in part, but here assumere means to take in or ingest a substance, and it also means to hire.

assunzione.t: Not "assumption" here: assunzione is the taking in of a substance, the noun of assumere, to consume; it also means hiring. Both words come from Latin assumptio, from assumere, to take up or take to oneself; Italian kept the literal taking, while English "assumption" came to mean taking something for granted.

attaccato.t: Not "attacked": attaccato here means attached or fastened. The English "attack" came through French from the Italian phrase attaccare battaglia, to join battle, and it is a twin of "attach", which carries the fastening sense that Italian uses here.

attende.t: Not "attend" in the sense of being present: here attendere means to wait or to wait for. Both come from Latin attendere, literally to stretch toward, that is, to turn the mind toward something; Old French and Italian kept "to wait for", while English went on to "to be present at".

attendere.t: Not "attend" in the sense of being present: here attendere means to wait or to wait for. Both come from Latin attendere, literally to stretch toward, that is, to turn the mind toward something; Old French and Italian kept "to wait for", while English went on to "to be present at".

attenersi.t: From the Latin attinere, made of ad- and tenere: attenersi a means to stick to or abide by a rule or instruction.

atterraggio.t: From terra: atterrare is to come down to earth, and atterraggio, through the French atterrage, is a landing.

attesa.t: From attendere (to wait): the attesa is the wait itself.

atti.t: Not "acts" here: in atti a, atti means suited to. This atto is a different word from atto, act: it comes from Latin aptus, fit, the source of English "apt", while the noun comes from Latin actus, from agere, to drive or to act.

attorno.t: From a and torno, a turn or circuit: around, in a circle.

attraversa.t: From attraverso, a traverso: to go across. The English "traverse" comes from the same Latin transversus.

attraversamento.t: From attraverso, a traverso: to go across. The English "traverse" comes from the same Latin transversus.

attraversando.t: From attraverso, a traverso: to go across. The English "traverse" comes from the same Latin transversus.

attraversano.t: From attraverso, a traverso: to go across. The English "traverse" comes from the same Latin transversus.

attraversare.t: From attraverso, a traverso: to go across. The English "traverse" comes from the same Latin transversus.

attraversarla.t: From attraverso, a traverso: to go across. The English "traverse" comes from the same Latin transversus.

attraversata.t: From attraverso, a traverso: to go across. The English "traverse" comes from the same Latin transversus.

attraverseranno.t: From attraverso, a traverso: to go across. The English "traverse" comes from the same Latin transversus.

attraversino.t: From attraverso, a traverso: to go across. The English "traverse" comes from the same Latin transversus.

attraverso.t: From a traverso (across): through or across. The English "traverse" comes from the same Latin transversus.

attrezzata.t: Picture a workshop full of attrezzi (tools): attrezzato means equipped, and attrezzature is the equipment.

attrezzature.t: Picture a workshop full of attrezzi (tools): attrezzato means equipped, and attrezzature is the equipment.

attrito.t: Close to the English "attrition" in its older sense, the rubbing of one thing against another: attrito means friction, as between a tire and the road.

attuare.t: Related to the English "actuate": attuare means to put into action, to carry out.

auricolare.t: From the Latin auricula, the ear, built on auris: the piece worn in the ear, an earpiece.

ausilio.t: Related to the English "auxiliary": both come from the Latin auxilium, help.

autista.t: Not "artist": autista is a driver, often one who drives for others. It is built from auto, short for automobile, plus -ista, an ending for a person who does something, so the word names the car person. It can also mean autistic, but not in these questions.

autoarticolato.t: From auto and articolato (jointed, as in "articulated"): a truck in two jointed parts.

autocaravan.t: From auto and caravan (travel trailer): a travel trailer that drives itself, a motorhome.

autocarro.t: Not a "car": autocarro, from auto (as in automobile) and carro (wagon), is a truck, a motor vehicle built to carry goods. Carro and the English "car" both come from Latin carrus, a wagon, so picture a motorized wagon for goods.

autocertifichi.t: From auto- (self) and certificare (to certify): to certify something about oneself, on one's own responsibility.

autocisterne.t: From auto and cisterna (tank, as in the English "cistern"): a tanker truck.

autodemolitore.t: Taken from autodemolizione, the demolition of cars: an autodemolitore is the business that breaks up and scraps old vehicles.

autolavaggi.t: From auto and lavaggio (a washing): a car wash. The English "lavatory" comes from the Latin lavare, to wash.

autolavaggio.t: From auto and lavaggio (a washing): a car wash. The English "lavatory" comes from the Latin lavare, to wash.

autorimessa.t: From auto and rimessa (a place where things are put away, from rimettere): a garage.

autosnodato.t: From auto and snodato: a vehicle built of several linked sections, one of them with the engine, such as a bus that bends in the middle.

autospazzatrici.t: From auto and spazzatrice: a motor vehicle equipped to clean the streets, a street sweeper.

autotreno.t: From auto and treno (train): a truck pulling a trailer, like a short train on the road.

autovelox.t: From auto and velox (Latin for fast, as in "velocity"): a speed camera.

autovettura.t: From auto and vettura (carriage, from the Latin vehere, to carry, as in "vehicle"): a passenger car.

avvalersi.t: From a- and valere (to be worth), the Latin source of the English "value": avvalersi means to avail oneself of something, to make use of it.

avvenga.t: From the Latin advenire (to come to), also the source of the English "advent": avvenire means to happen or to take place.

avvengono.t: From the Latin advenire (to come to), also the source of the English "advent": avvenire means to happen or to take place.

avvenire.t: From the Latin advenire (to come to), also the source of the English "advent": avvenire means to happen or to take place.

avvenuto.t: From the Latin advenire (to come to), also the source of the English "advent": avvenire means to happen or to take place.

avverte.t: Not "avert": avvertire means to warn someone, and also to notice or feel something, while "avert" means to turn away or prevent. The two differ by one Latin prefix: avvertire comes from advertere, to turn toward, that is, to turn attention to something, and "avert" from avertere, to turn away. In meaning it is close to "alert", though the two are unrelated: "alert" comes from the Italian all'erta, on the lookout.

avvertire.t: Not "avert": avvertire means to warn someone, and also to notice or feel something, while "avert" means to turn away or prevent. The two differ by one Latin prefix: avvertire comes from advertere, to turn toward, that is, to turn attention to something, and "avert" from avertere, to turn away. In meaning it is close to "alert", though the two are unrelated: "alert" comes from the Italian all'erta, on the lookout.

avviamento.t: From a- and via (way): to set something on its way, to start it.

avviare.t: From a- and via (way): to set something on its way, to start it.

avvicina.t: From vicino (near, as in "vicinity"): to bring or come near.

avvicinamento.t: From vicino (near, as in "vicinity"): to bring or come near.

avvicinando.t: From vicino (near, as in "vicinity"): to bring or come near.

avvicinandosi.t: From vicino (near, as in "vicinity"): to bring or come near.

avvicinarsi.t: From vicino (near, as in "vicinity"): to bring or come near.

avviene.t: From the Latin advenire (to come to), also the source of the English "advent": avvenire means to happen or to take place.

avvisare.t: Related to the English "advise", both from the Old French aviser: avvisare means to notify or warn someone, to let them know, rather than to give counsel.

avvisarlo.t: Related to the English "advise", both from the Old French aviser: avvisare means to notify or warn someone, to let them know, rather than to give counsel.

avvisato.t: Related to the English "advise", both from the Old French aviser: avvisare means to notify or warn someone, to let them know, rather than to give counsel.

avvistabile.t: From vista (sight, as in "vista"): to catch sight of something.

avvistamento.t: From vista (sight, as in "vista"): to catch sight of something.

avvistare.t: From vista (sight, as in "vista"): to catch sight of something.

avvistato.t: From vista (sight, as in "vista"): to catch sight of something.

avvolgendolo.t: From the Latin advolvere, reshaped to match the Italian volgere: avvolgere means to wrap something, or to wind it around something else.

azionabile.t: Borrowed from the French actionner: to set something in action, to make a machine or device work.

azionamento.t: Borrowed from the French actionner: to set something in action, to make a machine or device work.

azionando.t: Borrowed from the French actionner: to set something in action, to make a machine or device work.

azionare.t: Borrowed from the French actionner: to set something in action, to make a machine or device work.

azionato.t: Borrowed from the French actionner: to set something in action, to make a machine or device work.

azoto.t: Borrowed from the French azote, which was built from Greek parts meaning without and life.

azzeramento.t: From zero: azzerare is to bring something back to zero.

balneare.t: From the Latin balneum (bath): having to do with sea bathing and beach resorts.

banchina.t: From banco (bench) plus the ending -ina: a narrow strip, like a little bench, alongside the roadway. The same word also means a quay.

baricentro.t: From bari-, a Greek prefix for weight also seen in "barometer", and centro: the center of weight.

battistrada.t: From battere (to beat) and strada (road): the part of the tire that beats the road.

bendargli.t: From a Germanic word meaning band or bind: a benda is a bandage or a blindfold, and bendare is to put one on.

bendarglielo.t: From a Germanic word meaning band or bind: a benda is a bandage or a blindfold, and bendare is to put one on.

benzina.t: Not "benzene": benzina is gasoline, though both names come from the German Benzin. A German chemist coined Benzin for a liquid he obtained from benzoic acid; English reshaped the word into benzene for that chemical, while in Italian benzina became the name of the fuel.

bevande.t: Related to the English "beverage": both come from the Latin bibere, to drink.

binari.t: From the Latin binarius, built on a Latin word for two, which also gives "binary": a track is a pair of rails.

binario.t: From the Latin binarius, built on a Latin word for two, which also gives "binary": a track is a pair of rails.

bivio.t: From bi- (two) and via (way): the point where one road becomes two.

bollo.t: From the Latin bulla: a bollo is a stamp or seal, and here the vehicle tax, short for bollo auto.

bombolette.t: A diminutive of bombola: a small cylinder of compressed gas, and here a spray can.

brecciolino.t: Compare breccia, crushed stone for roads, the source of the English geology word "breccia": a brecciolino is gravel for roadmaking.

brividi.t: Sounds like "brr": brividi are the shivers or chills.

buche.t: Related to buco (hole): a buca is a hole or a pit.

caccia.t: Related to the English "chase" and "catch": all go back to the Late Latin captiare.

calda.t: Not "cold": calda means hot or warm. It comes from Latin calidus, warm, the same Latin word that gave English "cauldron", a large pot for heating.

calore.t: From the Latin calor (heat); the Italian caloria (calorie) is a related word.

calotta.t: Picture a skullcap: a calotta is a cap or cover, here the outer shell of a helmet.

calzature.t: From the Latin calceatura, built in Italian on calzare plus -tura: footwear, shoes.

campeggiare.t: From campo plus the verb ending -eggiare: campeggiare means to camp.

campeggio.t: From campo plus the verb ending -eggiare: campeggiare means to camp.

cantonieri.t: Borrowed from the French cantonnier: a worker who inspects and looks after a road or a railroad track.

capannoni.t: An augmentative of capanna, with the enlarging ending -one: a large shed, barn or hangar.

caravan.t: Not a "caravan" of travelers crossing a desert: here caravan means a travel trailer towed behind a vehicle. Italian took the word from English, where it first named a group of desert travelers, from Persian karwan, and later a covered carriage. In British English it names a camper, and that is the sense Italian uses.

carburante.t: As a noun, carburante means fuel; it is also the present participle of the verb carburare.

carceri.t: From the Latin carcer: a carcere is a jail or a prison.

caricare.t: From the Late Latin carricare, built on carrus, the source of carro (cart): to load. It also means to charge, as a battery is charged.

carichi.t: From the Late Latin carricare, built on carrus, the source of carro (cart): to load. It also means to charge, as a battery is charged.

carico.t: From the Late Latin carricare, built on carrus, the source of carro (cart): to load. It also means to charge, as a battery is charged.

carreggiata.t: Related to carreggiare (to cart), built on carro (cart): the carriageway, the part of the road used by vehicles.

carrello.t: A diminutive of carro (cart, wagon): a small cart, a trolley or a hand truck.

carri.t: From the Latin carrus: a carro is a wagon, cart or truck.

carro-attrezzi.t: Literally "cart with tools", from carro and attrezzi: a tow truck, fitted with winches and chains.

carrozzati.t: From carrozza (carriage): carrozzato means fitted with a body.

carrozzella.t: A diminutive of carrozza (carriage): it can mean a cab, a wheelchair or a motorcycle sidecar.

carrozzeria.t: From carrozza (carriage): the body of a vehicle, and also the body shop that repairs it.

cartelli.t: From carta: a sign, notice or placard. English "cartel" goes back to this word, by way of French and German.

caschi.t: Sounds like "cask": picture a hard cask worn over the head.

casco.t: Sounds like "cask": picture a hard cask worn over the head.

caserma.t: Borrowed from the French caserne: a caserma is a barracks.

cassonetti.t: Built from cassone plus the ending -etto: a street trash can or dumpster.

casuali.t: Not "casual" in the sense of relaxed: casuale means accidental or random, happening by chance (caso). Both come from Late Latin casualis, by chance, from casus, a chance event; English "casual" first meant the same and only later came to mean informal, while "casualty" still carries the old sense of an accident.

catadiottro.t: Related to the English optics term "catadioptric": a catadiottro is a reflector, like a cat's eye.

catena.t: From the Latin catena: a chain, and figuratively a bond or tie.

cavalcavia.t: From cavalcare (here, to span) and via (road): a road that spans another road, an overpass.

cavalletti.t: From cavallo (horse) with the ending -etto: a stand such as a sawhorse, and on a motorcycle the kickstand.

caviglia.t: By way of Occitan, from the Latin clavicula, a diminutive of clavis (key); the Italian clavicola is a doublet from the same Latin word.

cavo.t: This cavo, meaning cable, rope or wire, probably came through the Portuguese cabo from the Latin capulum. A different cavo means hollow.

cerchioni.t: From cerchio (circle) with the enlarging ending -one: the rim of a wheel.

chiodi.t: From the Latin clavus: a chiodo is a nail, a stud or a spike.

ciclomotore.t: Built from ciclo and motore, on the model of the French cyclomoteur: a moped.

ciclomotorista.t: From ciclomotore (moped) plus -ista, an ending for people: a moped rider.

ciclopedonale.t: From ciclo (bicycle) and pedonale (for pedestrians): for bicycles and pedestrians together.

cifra.t: From the Arabic sifr (zero, empty), the same source as the Italian zero. It can mean a cipher, but here it means a figure or a sum.

cilindrata.t: Picture the cylinders of an engine: cilindrata is the engine's cubic capacity, its displacement.

cingolate.t: From cingolo, a caterpillar track, borrowed from the Latin cingulum (a belt or sash): fitted with caterpillar tracks.

ciondoli.t: Related to ciondolare (to dangle): something that hangs and swings, such as a charm.

circola.t: Related to the English "circulate", both from the Latin circulare: on the road circolare means to travel or be driven, the way traffic circulates.

circolando.t: Related to the English "circulate", both from the Latin circulare: on the road circolare means to travel or be driven, the way traffic circulates.

circolano.t: Related to the English "circulate", both from the Latin circulare: on the road circolare means to travel or be driven, the way traffic circulates.

circolanti.t: Related to the English "circulate", both from the Latin circulare: on the road circolare means to travel or be driven, the way traffic circulates.

circolare.t: Related to the English "circulate", both from the Latin circulare: on the road circolare means to travel or be driven, the way traffic circulates.

circolazione.t: Related to the English "circulation", both from the Latin circulationem: here circolazione means road traffic, the movement of vehicles.

cisterne.t: The same word as the English "cistern", both from the Latin cisterna, a tank for liquid: here cisterna is a tank truck, or the tank it carries.

clacson.t: Borrowed from the English "klaxon": a car horn.

climatizzatore.t: Built from climatizzare plus -tore: an air conditioner, informally called clima.

cogliere.t: From the Latin colligere: cogliere means to pick or gather, and also to grasp.

coinvolto.t: The past participle of coinvolgere, to involve or implicate: coinvolto means involved.

collaudo.t: From the Latin collaudare, made of con- and laudare (to praise): a collaudo is a test that a vehicle or device is put through.

colle.t: Plural of colla (glue), related to English "collage", a picture made by gluing.

collega.t: Not "colleague" here: this collega is a form of collegare, to connect or link, from the Latin colligare. Colligare means to bind together, from ligare, to tie, the root of English "ligament"; the noun collega, colleague, is a separate word from Latin collega, one chosen to serve alongside another.

collegamento.t: From collegare (to connect), which goes back to Latin ligare (to tie), the root of "ligament": a connection or link.

collegato.t: Not "colleague" here: this collega is a form of collegare, to connect or link, from the Latin colligare. Colligare means to bind together, from ligare, to tie, the root of English "ligament"; the noun collega, colleague, is a separate word from Latin collega, one chosen to serve alongside another.

collocare.t: From con- and the Latin locare (to place), the root of English "locate": to put something in position.

collocarlo.t: From con- and the Latin locare (to place), the root of English "locate": to put something in position.

collocato.t: From con- and the Latin locare (to place), the root of English "locate": to put something in position.

colonnina.t: Diminutive of colonna (column): a small post or bollard.

colorito.t: Think of the English "coloring": as a noun, colorito is the color of a person's face, the complexion.

commisurare.t: Related to English "commensurate": built on misura (measure), it means to size one thing in proportion to another.

commisurata.t: Related to English "commensurate": built on misura (measure), it means to size one thing in proportion to another.

compaia.t: Subjunctive of comparire (to appear), which shares the Latin parere (to be visible) with English "appear".

comparsa.t: From comparire (to appear): the moment something shows up, its appearance or onset.

compie.t: From the Latin complere (to fill up), the source of English "complete": to carry something through to its end.

compiere.t: From the Latin complere (to fill up), the source of English "complete": to carry something through to its end.

compiersi.t: From the Latin complere (to fill up), the source of English "complete": to carry something through to its end.

compimento.t: From compiere (to complete, from the Latin complere): the completion or fulfillment of something.

compiono.t: From the Latin complere (to fill up), the source of English "complete": to carry something through to its end.

compiuto.t: From the Latin complere (to fill up), the source of English "complete": to carry something through to its end.

complessiva.t: Not "complex": complessivo means overall or total, everything taken together. Both come from Latin complexus, from complecti, to encircle or embrace; Italian kept the sense of embracing all the parts at once, while English "complex" came to mean intricate.

complesso.t: The same word as the English noun "complex", both from the Latin complexus: complesso is a whole made of joined parts, like a building complex or a combination of vehicles.

comporta.t: Not "comport": comportare means to entail or bring with it, as an act brings a consequence. Both come from Latin comportare, to carry together, from com (together) and portare (to carry); Italian kept the idea of carrying something along, while English "comport" came to mean how one carries oneself, that is, behaves.

comportano.t: Not "comport": comportare means to entail or bring with it, as an act brings a consequence. Both come from Latin comportare, to carry together, from com (together) and portare (to carry); Italian kept the idea of carrying something along, while English "comport" came to mean how one carries oneself, that is, behaves.

comportare.t: Not "comport": comportare means to entail or bring with it, as an act brings a consequence. Both come from Latin comportare, to carry together, from com (together) and portare (to carry); Italian kept the idea of carrying something along, while English "comport" came to mean how one carries oneself, that is, behaves.

comportino.t: Not "comport": comportare means to entail or bring with it, as an act brings a consequence. Both come from Latin comportare, to carry together, from com (together) and portare (to carry); Italian kept the idea of carrying something along, while English "comport" came to mean how one carries oneself, that is, behaves.

comprende.t: Like "comprehend" in part, but in these questions comprendere means to include or comprise.

comprendere.t: Like "comprehend" in part, but in these questions comprendere means to include or comprise.

comprenderne.t: Like "comprehend" in part, but in these questions comprendere means to include or comprise.

compreso.t: Compreso can mean understood, as "comprehended" does, but here it usually means included, and compreso tra means included between two limits.

comune.t: Not "common" here: as a noun, il comune is the municipality, the town and its government. The noun is Latin commune, the adjective communis, common or shared, used as a noun for what a community holds in common; the English "commune", a self-governing local community, comes from the same Latin adjective.

concessionario.t: Not a "concession" stand: a concessionario is an agent or dealer, such as a car dealership. It comes from concessione, a right granted, from Latin concedere, to yield or grant; the concessionario is the one who holds a granted right, and the English stand is named for the same kind of grant, a lease of a small space.

condotte.t: Related to the English "conduct", both from the Latin conducere, to lead: condotto is the participle of condurre, which in these questions means to drive a vehicle.

conduce.t: Related to the English "conduct", both from the Latin conducere, to lead: conduce is a form of condurre, which means to lead, and here to drive a vehicle.

conducente.t: Related to the English "conductor", first "one who leads or guides", from the Latin conducere: the conducente is the driver of the vehicle, not a train conductor who collects fares.

conducibili.t: Not "conducive": conducibile is formed on condurre and means able to be conducted or led; in these questions, able to be driven. Both go back to Latin conducere, to lead together; Italian built conducibile on the plain sense of leading, while English "conducive" grew from a later sense of helping toward a result.

condurre.t: Related to the English "conduct", both from the Latin conducere, to lead: conduce is a form of condurre, which means to lead, and here to drive a vehicle.

conficcati.t: From con- and ficcare (to thrust in): driven in and stuck fast.

confine.t: Related to the English "confines", the limits of a place, both from the Latin confinis: il confine is a border or boundary, such as the edge of a piece of land.

confronti.t: Not "confront": nei confronti di means toward someone, and a confronto is often a comparison. Both go back to Medieval Latin confrontare, built on frons (forehead, front); Italian confrontare puts two things face to face in order to compare them, while English "confront" came to mean facing someone in opposition.

consapevole.t: From consapere, built from con- and sapere (to know): consapevole means informed of something, aware of it.

consegnare.t: Related to English "consign": both mean to hand something over to someone.

consegnarlo.t: Related to English "consign": both mean to hand something over to someone.

consegue.t: As a transitive verb conseguire means to obtain or achieve, as in obtaining a license, a sense the English "consequence" does not carry.

conseguimento.t: Not "consequence": conseguimento means the obtaining of something, from conseguire, to obtain. Both go back to Latin consequi, to follow after, which also meant to overtake and to obtain; Italian conseguire kept "to obtain", while English "consequence" kept "what follows".

conseguire.t: As a transitive verb conseguire means to obtain or achieve, as in obtaining a license, a sense the English "consequence" does not carry.

conseguita.t: As a transitive verb conseguire means to obtain or achieve, as in obtaining a license, a sense the English "consequence" does not carry.

consenso.t: Related to the English "consensus" and "consent", from the Latin consentire, to agree: consenso here is one person's consent or permission, not the agreement of a whole group.

consente.t: Related to the English "consent", both from the Latin consentire: consentire means to allow or permit, and è consentito means it is permitted.

consentire.t: Related to the English "consent", both from the Latin consentire: consentire means to allow or permit, and è consentito means it is permitted.

consentito.t: Related to the English "consent", both from the Latin consentire: consentire means to allow or permit, and è consentito means it is permitted.

consentono.t: Related to the English "consent", both from the Latin consentire: consentire means to allow or permit, and è consentito means it is permitted.

consiglia.t: From the Latin consilium, the source of English "counsel": to advise or recommend.

consigliabile.t: From consigliare (to advise, related to English "counsel"): advisable, recommended.

consigliare.t: From the Latin consilium, the source of English "counsel": to advise or recommend.

consigliargli.t: From the Latin consilium, the source of English "counsel": to advise or recommend.

consigliata.t: From the Latin consilium, the source of English "counsel": to advise or recommend.

contachilometri.t: From contare (to count) and chilometri (kilometers): the counter of kilometers traveled.

contemplate.t: Related to the English "contemplate", both from the Latin contemplari, to consider: said of a law, contemplare means to take a case into consideration, that is, to provide for it.

contempo.t: From con- and tempo (time): nel contempo means at the same time.

contemporaneamente.t: Related to the English "contemporaneous", both from the Latin contemporaneus: contemporaneamente means at the same time, simultaneously.

contestualmente.t: Not "contextually" here: in these statements contestualmente means at the same time, in the same act. Like "context", it goes back to Latin contextus, a joining together, from contexere, to weave together; Italian legal usage applied the idea to one act joined in time to another.

contraddistingue.t: Built on distinguere (to distinguish): to mark something so that it can be told apart.

contraddistinguere.t: Built on distinguere (to distinguish): to mark something so that it can be told apart.

contraddistinta.t: Built on distinguere (to distinguish): to mark something so that it can be told apart.

contraffatte.t: From contra- and fare (to make): made in imitation, from the same Latin origin as English "counterfeit".

contrassegna.t: From contrassegno, itself from contra- and segno (sign, mark): contrassegnare means to put an identifying mark on something.

contrassegnata.t: From contrassegno, itself from contra- and segno (sign, mark): contrassegnare means to put an identifying mark on something.

contrassegno.t: From contra- and segno (sign, mark): a mark or badge that identifies something.

controsole.t: Contro means against and sole means sun; the two are joined into one word, the same way contro vento becomes controvento, against the wind.

conveniente.t: Not "convenient" in the sense of handy: in these statements conveniente means advisable or worthwhile, the better thing to do. Both come from Latin conveniens, from convenire, to come together or to suit; English "convenient" once also meant fit or appropriate, the sense Italian kept.

convenzione.t: Related to the English "convention" in its sense of a formal agreement between states: convenzione means an agreement or pact.

conviene.t: Not "convenient": conviene is a verb meaning it is advisable, one had better, the better course. It comes from Latin convenire, to come together, agree, or be fitting, the source of "convenient", which in English first meant fitting or proper and later narrowed to easy or handy.

convogliare.t: Related to English "convoy": to channel things or carry them along together.

cordolo.t: Picture a cord laid along the edge of the road: a cordolo is a raised strip, such as a curb.

corredato.t: Built on the same Germanic root as arredare (to furnish): corredare means to supply something with what it needs, such as documents attached to it.

corridori.t: Not "corridors": corridori are runners or racers, from correre, to run. English "corridor" came through French from this same Italian word, which once also named a long passage in a building; the word itself means "a runner".

corsia.t: Once the word for a stream of running water, corsia now names a long strip set apart for movement, such as a lane of a road.

corteo.t: Related to English "cortege": both name a procession of people moving together.

cortili.t: From corte (court): an open court enclosed by buildings, a courtyard.

cosiddetti.t: From così (so) and detto (said): literally "so said", the same idea as the English "so-called".

costretti.t: From costringere, from the Latin constringere (to bind tightly), the source of the English "constrain" and "constrict": to force.

costringe.t: From costringere, from the Latin constringere (to bind tightly), the source of the English "constrain" and "constrict": to force.

costringerlo.t: From costringere, from the Latin constringere (to bind tightly), the source of the English "constrain" and "constrict": to force.

costruttive.t: Not "constructive" in the sense of helpful: here costruttivo means having to do with how a thing is built, its design or structure. Both come from Latin construere, to pile up together; English "constructive" has a rare building sense too, but its everyday meaning became helpful, while Italian uses the building sense freely in technical writing.

costruttore.t: Related to the English "constructor", a builder: costruttore here is the maker of a vehicle or device, its manufacturer.

crocevia.t: From croce (cross) and via (road): the place where roads cross.

custoditi.t: From custodire (to guard), the same root as the English "custody" and "custodian": watched over, kept under guard.

danneggiamento.t: From danno (harm), from the Latin damnum, the source of the English "damage": danneggiare means to cause damage.

danneggiano.t: From danno (harm), from the Latin damnum, the source of the English "damage": danneggiare means to cause damage.

danneggiare.t: From danno (harm), from the Latin damnum, the source of the English "damage": danneggiare means to cause damage.

danneggiato.t: From danno (harm), from the Latin damnum, the source of the English "damage": danneggiare means to cause damage.

danno.t: From the Latin damnum (loss, harm), the source of the English "damage": a danno is damage or harm.

dannosi.t: From the Latin damnosus: dannoso means harmful, causing danno, a word from the Latin damnum, the source of the English "damage".

decollo.t: Taken from the French décoller (to unstick): the decollo is the moment an aircraft comes unstuck from the ground.

decurtati.t: From de- and the Latin curtus (shortened), the root of the English "curt": decurtare means to cut down or deduct.

definitivamente.t: Not "definitely": definitivamente means permanently, once and for all, in the sense of "definitive" (final). Both go back to Latin definire, to set bounds, from finis, an end; Italian follows "definitive", having the character of finality, while English "definitely" came to mean certainly.

denuncia.t: Not a "denunciation" here: a denuncia is a formal report or notice to an authority. Latin denuntiare meant to announce officially, which English "denounce" also meant before it came to mean condemn.

denunzia.t: Not a "denunciation" here: a denuncia is a formal report or notice to an authority. Latin denuntiare meant to announce officially, which English "denounce" also meant before it came to mean condemn.

detergere.t: From the Latin detergere (to wipe away), the verb behind the English "detergent": detergere means to clean or wipe a surface.

determinare.t: Like "determine" in part, but determinare often means to cause or bring about, and determinato often means a specific or certain one.

determinata.t: Like "determine" in part, but determinare often means to cause or bring about, and determinato often means a specific or certain one.

detersivi.t: From the same Latin root as the English "detergent" (detergere, to wipe clean): detersivo is the everyday word for a cleaning product.

difficilmente.t: Besides "with difficulty", difficilmente often means unlikely or hardly, as in something that will hardly happen. It is difficile plus the adverb ending -mente, and difficile goes back to Latin difficilis, from dis- (not) and facilis (easy), the source of the English "difficulty".

direttrice.t: The feminine of direttore, used as an adjective meaning giving direction: the ruote direttrici are the wheels linked to the steering, not the steering wheel itself.

dirigendosi.t: From dirigersi, to head somewhere or make one's way toward a place: dirigendosi means heading toward.

dirigibilità.t: Related to dirigibile, able to be directed, from dirigere (to direct). As a noun, dirigibile is also the airship, a balloon that can be steered.

disappannamento.t: From dis- (removing) and appannare (to fog up), itself from panno (cloth): to clear the mist from the glass.

disappannare.t: From dis- (removing) and appannare (to fog up), itself from panno (cloth): to clear the mist from the glass.

discarica.t: From discaricare, an older form of scaricare (to unload): a discarica is the place where waste is unloaded and left, a dump.

disciplinata.t: Said of traffic or a crossing, disciplinato means regulated, run in order under set rules, rather than "disciplined" in the sense of well behaved.

discretamente.t: Related to the English "discreet": discretamente here means with moderation and restraint, not loudly or insistently.

disinserire.t: From dis- (undoing) and inserire (to insert): to disconnect a machine or cut the current, taking a device out of operation.

dislivelli.t: From dis- (difference) and livello (level): a difference in height between two surfaces.

dispone.t: Not "dispose of": disporre means to place or arrange, disporsi to place oneself, and disporre di to have available. Both come from Latin disponere, to put in order, from dis-, apart, and ponere, to place; English "dispose" first meant the same, to set in order, a sense still heard in "disposition".

disporre.t: Not "dispose of": disporre means to place or arrange, disporsi to place oneself, and disporre di to have available. Both come from Latin disponere, to put in order, from dis-, apart, and ponere, to place; English "dispose" first meant the same, to set in order, a sense still heard in "disposition".

disporsi.t: Not "dispose of": disporre means to place or arrange, disporsi to place oneself, and disporre di to have available. Both come from Latin disponere, to put in order, from dis-, apart, and ponere, to place; English "dispose" first meant the same, to set in order, a sense still heard in "disposition".

dispositivo.t: From Latin dispositus (arranged), the participle behind disporre; the sense of device came through the French dispositif, a mechanism that serves a set function.

disposizione.t: Related to the English "disposition" in its old sense of arrangement: disposizione is an arrangement or layout, and a disposizione means at one's disposal, available.

disposto.t: Besides "disposed" (inclined), disposto means placed or positioned, as the past participle of disporre (to place, to arrange).

dissestato.t: Made as the opposite of assestare (to settle in place): dissestare means to knock out of sesto, out of proper order, so a strada dissestata is a broken-up road.

dista.t: From distare (to be distant), the verb behind the English "distant": a place that dista a certain amount is that far away.

distano.t: From distare (to be distant), the verb behind the English "distant": a place that dista a certain amount is that far away.

distesa.t: Participle of distendere (to stretch out), related to the English "distend": lying stretched out.

distributore.t: Besides a "distributor" of goods, distributore di carburante, or just distributore, is a fuel pump, and by extension the gas station where it stands.

diversa.t: Not "diverse" in the sense of varied: in these statements diverso means different, other than the one named, as in salvo diversa indicazione, unless otherwise indicated. Both come from Latin diversus, literally turned in another direction, from divertere, to turn aside, which is why diverso points to something other than the one named.

divieto.t: From divietare, a rare form of vietare (to forbid): a divieto is a ban, a prohibition imposed by an authority.

dogana.t: From the Arabic diwan (register, office), the same word behind the English "divan": dogana means customs.

dorso.t: From the Latin dorsum (back), the root of the English "dorsal": the back of something, such as the hand.

dosso.t: From dossum, a popular Latin form of dorsum (back), like dorso: a dosso is a hump, the high point of a rise in the road.

dotato.t: From dotare (to endow), from the Latin dos (dowry), the root of the English "dowry" and "endow": provided with, equipped.

dovuti.t: Participle of dovere (to owe, must); dovuto a means owed to, and so caused by, much like the English "due to".

effettua.t: From effetto (effect), modeled on the French effectuer: effettuare means to put into effect, to carry out.

effettuano.t: From effetto (effect), modeled on the French effectuer: effettuare means to put into effect, to carry out.

effettuare.t: From effetto (effect), modeled on the French effectuer: effettuare means to put into effect, to carry out.

effettuarla.t: From effetto (effect), modeled on the French effectuer: effettuare means to put into effect, to carry out.

effettuarsi.t: From effetto (effect), modeled on the French effectuer: effettuare means to put into effect, to carry out.

effettuata.t: From effetto (effect), modeled on the French effectuer: effettuare means to put into effect, to carry out.

effettuazione.t: From effetto (effect), modeled on the French effectuer: effettuare means to put into effect, to carry out.

efficaci.t: Related to the English "efficacious": efficace means effective, producing the result that is wanted.

efficiente.t: Related to the English "efficient": said of a vehicle or device, efficiente means working as it should, in good working order.

efficienza.t: Related to the English "efficiency": said of a vehicle or device, efficienza means good working order, the condition of working as it should.

ente.t: From the Latin ens, entis (a being), the root of the English "entity": an ente is a public body or authority.

entro.t: Entro means within or no later than, and it sets a limit, usually of time, that is not to be passed.

equiparato.t: From the Latin aequiparare: equiparare means to put two things on a par, so equiparato means treated as equal to another thing.

eroina.t: Not "heroine": eroina here is heroin, the drug, although the same spelling also means a heroine. The two look alike because the drug's name, first a German trademark, was built on the word for hero, reportedly for the euphoria the drug brings.

esegue.t: From the Latin exsequi, to follow out, the same source as the English "execute": eseguire means to carry something out.

eseguire.t: From the Latin exsequi, to follow out, the same source as the English "execute": eseguire means to carry something out.

eseguirla.t: From the Latin exsequi, to follow out, the same source as the English "execute": eseguire means to carry something out.

eseguirne.t: From the Latin exsequi, to follow out, the same source as the English "execute": eseguire means to carry something out.

eseguito.t: From the Latin exsequi, to follow out, the same source as the English "execute": eseguire means to carry something out.

esigenze.t: From the late Latin exigentia, the source of the English "exigency", something that is needed: esigenze are needs or requirements.

esporre.t: Related to the English "expose" in its sense of exhibit openly: esporre here means to display, to put a ticket or notice where it can be seen.

estate.t: Not "estate": estate means summer. It comes from Latin aestas, a word built on aestus (heat), while the English "estate" is unrelated and goes back to Latin status, condition or standing.

estivo.t: From the Latin aestivus, from aestus (heat, summer), the same root as estate (summer): estivo means of the summer.

eventuale.t: Not "eventual": eventuale means possible or any that may occur, something that might happen rather than something that will happen in the end. It is built on evento, event, so it means depending on events; English "eventual" also first meant "pertaining to events" and only later came to mean "ultimately resulting", while "eventuality", a possible occurrence, keeps the older sense.

eventualmente.t: Not "eventually": eventualmente means if need be or possibly, in case the situation arises. Both words go back to Latin evenire, to come out or happen, through evento and event; Italian kept the sense of whatever may happen, while English "eventual" later came to mean what results in the end.

evidenzia.t: Related to the English "evident": evidenziare means to highlight, to make a thing evident so that it stands out clearly.

evidenziare.t: Related to the English "evident": evidenziare means to highlight, to make a thing evident so that it stands out clearly.

evidenziato.t: Related to the English "evident": evidenziare means to highlight, to make a thing evident so that it stands out clearly.

fabbrica.t: Not "fabric": fabbrica means factory, a place where things are made. Both come from Latin fabrica, a workshop; Italian kept the workshop, while English "fabric" moved from a building to anything made, then to manufactured material and finally to cloth.

facilità.t: Not "facility" as a building: facilità means ease, the quality of something that is facile (easy). Both come from Latin facilitas, ease; English "facility" also meant ease at first and only in the nineteenth century came to mean a place built for doing something.

facoltativo.t: Related to the English "faculty" in its old sense of power: facoltativo, from facoltà (an option or right), means optional, left to a person's free choice.

facoltà.t: Related to the English "faculty" in its sense of a power or ability: facoltà is an option or right to do something, or an ability, as in la facoltà di guida.

fanciulli.t: From fancello, a shortened diminutive of fante, an old word for a child that is infante (infant) with its first syllable dropped.

fango.t: From a Germanic word related to the Gothic fani (mud); the English "fen", a marshy land, comes from the same Germanic source.

fari.t: From Pharos, the lighthouse of Alexandria: a faro is a lighthouse, so a car's fari are its lighthouses.

fascia.t: From the Latin fascia (band); English borrowed the word for a band in architecture and for a band of tissue in anatomy.

fasciargli.t: Fasciare means to wrap in a fascia (band), that is, to bandage a wound or a limb.

fastidio.t: Not "fastidious": fastidio means annoyance or discomfort. Both come from Latin fastidium, loathing or distaste; Italian kept the feeling of being bothered by something, while English "fastidious" turned it toward the person who is hard to please.

fastidiosi.t: Not "fastidious" (fussy): here fastidioso means annoying, something that causes fastidio (annoyance). Both come from Latin fastidiosus, from fastidium, loathing or aversion; Italian took the side of the thing that causes the aversion, while English took the side of the person who feels it and is hard to please.

faticoso.t: From fatica (effort, weariness); the English "fatigue" shares the root.

fattoria.t: Not "factory": fattoria means farm; the Italian for factory is fabbrica. Fattoria comes from fattore, the agent who managed a landowner's farms; English "factory" also began as the office of such agents and only later came to mean a building for making goods.

ferita.t: From Latin ferire (to strike); the English "interfere" contains the same root.

ferite.t: From Latin ferire (to strike); the English "interfere" contains the same root.

feriti.t: From Latin ferire (to strike); the English "interfere" contains the same root.

ferito.t: From Latin ferire (to strike); the English "interfere" contains the same root.

ferroviario.t: From ferrovia, literally "iron way" (ferro, iron, and via, way), the Italian for railway.

fiancheggiato.t: From fianco (side, flank): to run along the side of something.

fianco.t: The same word as the English "flank": both come from the Old French flanc (side).

fiere.t: From Latin feria (holiday), the same source as the English "fair", a market or show.

filobus.t: From filo (wire) and bus: a bus that draws its power from overhead wires.

finestrella.t: Diminutive of finestra (window): a small window.

finestrini.t: Diminutive of finestra (window): the small windows of a car.

firma.t: Not "firm": firma means signature, from firmare (to sign), which comes from Latin firmare, to confirm. The English "firm", a company, came from this Italian word through the German Firma.

fissaggio.t: From fissare, modeled on the French fixage: fissaggio is the act of fastening something in place or making it stable.

fissare.t: From fissare, modeled on the French fixage: fissaggio is the act of fastening something in place or making it stable.

fissato.t: From fissare, modeled on the French fixage: fissaggio is the act of fastening something in place or making it stable.

fisso.t: From fissare, modeled on the French fixage: fissaggio is the act of fastening something in place or making it stable.

fitta.t: From the Latin fictus, a popular participle of figere (to drive in): things packed in tightly, as in fitta nebbia (thick fog).

fiume.t: From Latin flumen, from fluere (to flow), which is also the source of the English "flume", a channel for water.

fogliame.t: From foglia (leaf), from Latin folium; the English "foliage" came from the French word for leaf and was later reshaped after the same Latin folium.

foglie.t: From foglia (leaf), from Latin folium; the English "foliage" came from the French word for leaf and was later reshaped after the same Latin folium.

fondo.t: Besides "fund", fondo means bottom or background, as in su fondo verde, on a green background.

foratura.t: From forare (to pierce, make a hole); the English "perforate" shares the root.

fornici.t: From Latin fornix (arch or vault), a word English still uses in anatomy.

fornire.t: Related to the English "furnish", which first meant to supply or equip before it meant putting furniture in a room. Fornire le generalità is to supply your personal details.

forniscono.t: Related to the English "furnish", in its sense of to supply or provide.

forniti.t: Related to the English "furnish", in its sense of to supply or provide.

foro.t: From forare (to pierce, make a hole); the English "perforate" shares the root.

foschia.t: From fosco (dark, dim), Latin fuscus; the English "obfuscate", to darken or obscure, shares the root.

frecce.t: Freccia is an arrow; the turn signal kept the name from the arrow-shaped arm that older cars raised to the left or right before turning.

freccia.t: Freccia is an arrow; the turn signal kept the name from the arrow-shaped arm that older cars raised to the left or right before turning.

frenante.t: From Latin frenum, the bit and bridle that hold a horse back; the English verb "refrain", to hold back, comes from the same frenum.

frenare.t: From Latin frenum, the bit and bridle that hold a horse back; the English verb "refrain", to hold back, comes from the same frenum.

frenata.t: From Latin frenum, the bit and bridle that hold a horse back; the English verb "refrain", to hold back, comes from the same frenum.

frenatura.t: From Latin frenum, the bit and bridle that hold a horse back; the English verb "refrain", to hold back, comes from the same frenum.

freno.t: From Latin frenum, the bit and bridle that hold a horse back; the English verb "refrain", to hold back, comes from the same frenum.

frequenza.t: Not "frequency" here: frequenza also means going somewhere regularly, so the frequenza of a course is attendance at its classes. Both come from Latin frequentia, a crowding or gathering in great numbers; the Italian sense matches the English verb "to frequent" a place, meaning to visit it regularly.

frizione.t: Not "friction" here: frizione is the clutch, short for innesto a frizione, the device that connects the engine to the wheels or disconnects it. Both words come from Latin frictio, a rubbing, from fricare, to rub; Italian named the clutch after its friction coupling, while English "friction" kept only the sense of rubbing and resistance.

fronteggiare.t: From fronte (front): to stand face to face with something, to confront it.

fugge.t: From Latin fugere (to flee), the root of the English "fugitive" and "refuge".

fumo.t: From Latin fumus (smoke), the root of the English "fumes".

fune.t: From Latin funis (rope); the English "funicular", a railway pulled by a cable, shares the root.

fuoristrada.t: From fuori (outside) and strada (road): a vehicle made to go off the road.

fuoriuscita.t: From fuoriuscire (to come out): a fuoriuscita is the act of something coming out, such as a leak of liquid or gas.

furgonati.t: Related to furgone, a fully enclosed vehicle for carrying goods: furgonati are vans or van-type vehicles.

furto.t: From Latin furtum (theft); the English "furtive", done secretly like a thief, shares the root.

gabbia.t: From Latin cavea (enclosure), the root of the English "cage".

galleria.t: Besides a "gallery", on the road a galleria is a tunnel.

gareggia.t: From gara (a race or contest): to take part in a race.

gasolio.t: Adapted from the English "gas oil", gas plus oil: a petroleum fraction used as fuel for diesel engines.

gestire.t: Not "gesture" here: gestire means to manage or run, a back-formation from gestione (management). A rarer separate verb gestire does mean to gesticulate. Both trace back to Latin gerere, to carry or carry on: gestione comes from Latin gestio, managing, while "gesture" comes from gestus, the way a person carries the body.

gettare.t: From Latin iactare (to throw), which also lies behind the English "jettison".

ghiacciato.t: From Latin glacies (ice), the root of the English "glacier".

ghiaccio.t: From Latin glacies (ice), the root of the English "glacier".

giacche.t: Giacche is the plural of giacca, from Old French jaque; the English "jacket" comes from a diminutive of that same Old French word.

ginocchio.t: From Latin genu (knee), the root of the English "genuflect", to bend the knee.

giudice.t: From Latin iudex (judge). Compare the English "judicial", from Latin iudicialis.

giungendo.t: From Latin iungere (to join), the root of the English "junction": to arrive is to join the place one was heading for.

gode.t: From godere (to enjoy), Latin gaudere (to rejoice), which also gave the English "joy" through French.

gomito.t: From Latin cubitum, elbow. The English "cubit" is the same word, because a cubit was a length measured along the forearm from the elbow to the fingertip.

gomma.t: Not "gum" here: gomma means rubber, and by extension a tire, although the same word can also mean chewing gum. Gomma and "gum" both come from Latin gummi, a plant resin, which Latin took from Greek and Greek from Egyptian.

gommata.t: From gomma (rubber, tire): made or covered with rubber, as a wheel with a rubber tire is.

gommatura.t: From the verb gommare plus the suffix -tura; it names the tires fitted to a vehicle, and gomma is the word for a tire.

gommoni.t: From gomma (rubber) with the augmentative -one: a big rubber boat.

gonfia.t: From Latin conflare. Gonfiare means to inflate with air, and also to swell.

gonfiabile.t: From Latin conflare. Gonfiare means to inflate with air, and also to swell.

gonfiato.t: From Latin conflare. Gonfiare means to inflate with air, and also to swell.

gpl.t: The initials of gas di petrolio liquefatto, the Italian for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).

gradino.t: From grado plus the suffix -ino; grado comes from Latin gradus (step), the source of the English "grade" and "gradual".

grandinate.t: Grandine, from Latin grandinem, is hail, and a grandinata is a hailstorm. Picture grand, big stones of ice falling from the sky.

grandine.t: Grandine, from Latin grandinem, is hail, and a grandinata is a hailstorm. Picture grand, big stones of ice falling from the sky.

grava.t: Gravare, from Latin gravare, means to rest or weigh on something. Compare grave (heavy), from Latin gravis, the root of the English "gravity".

gravare.t: Gravare, from Latin gravare, means to rest or weigh on something. Compare grave (heavy), from Latin gravis, the root of the English "gravity".

guanto.t: From Frankish through Old French guant. The same Frankish word gave the French gant, whose diminutive gantelet became the English "gauntlet".

guantoni.t: Augmentative of guanto (glove), from the same source as the English "gauntlet": big gloves, such as boxing gloves.

guarnizioni.t: Built on guarnire, to fit out or equip, which comes from the same Germanic word as the English "garnish", a word that also first meant to fit out. A guarnizione is a part fitted into a machine: a seal between two surfaces, or the friction lining that the brakes and the clutch press against the metal.

guasto.t: From guastare (to ruin, to break), from Latin vastare, the source of the English "devastate". A guasto is a breakdown or fault.

idoneo.t: From Latin idoneus, which also gave the English word "idoneous", meaning appropriate or suitable.

ignifuga.t: From Latin ignis (fire), the root of the English "ignite", plus the ending -fugo: fireproof, or slow to catch fire.

imbarcazioni.t: From imbarcare, built on barca (boat); compare the English "embark", from French barque (small ship). An imbarcazione is any boat or craft.

imbarco.t: From imbarcare, built from im- and barca (boat): boarding or loading. Compare the English "embark", from French em- and barque (small ship).

imbocchi.t: From in- and bocca (mouth): to go into the mouth of a road, street or tunnel.

immatricolato.t: From matricola (an official register), as in the English "matriculate": to enter a vehicle in the official register.

immettano.t: From Latin immittere; compare the English "admit" and "emit", from Latin admittere and emittere. Immettersi is to enter, as into a flow of traffic.

immette.t: From Latin immittere; compare the English "admit" and "emit", from Latin admittere and emittere. Immettersi is to enter, as into a flow of traffic.

immettendosi.t: From Latin immittere; compare the English "admit" and "emit", from Latin admittere and emittere. Immettersi is to enter, as into a flow of traffic.

immettere.t: From Latin immittere; compare the English "admit" and "emit", from Latin admittere and emittere. Immettersi is to enter, as into a flow of traffic.

immettersi.t: From Latin immittere; compare the English "admit" and "emit", from Latin admittere and emittere. Immettersi is to enter, as into a flow of traffic.

immettono.t: From Latin immittere; compare the English "admit" and "emit", from Latin admittere and emittere. Immettersi is to enter, as into a flow of traffic.

immissione.t: From Latin immissio, from immittere (see immettere): the act of entering a road. Compare the English "admission", from Latin admissio.

impantanati.t: From pantano (a bog or swamp): stuck as if sunk in a bog.

impegna.t: From pegno (a pledge): to commit something, and on the road to commit the vehicle to a space such as an intersection.

impegnando.t: From pegno (a pledge): to commit something, and on the road to commit the vehicle to a space such as an intersection.

impegnare.t: From pegno (a pledge): to commit something, and on the road to commit the vehicle to a space such as an intersection.

impegnarlo.t: From pegno (a pledge): to commit something, and on the road to commit the vehicle to a space such as an intersection.

impegnativa.t: From impegnare (to commit, from pegno, a pledge): something that demands a great deal of commitment or effort.

impegnato.t: From pegno (a pledge): to commit something, and on the road to commit the vehicle to a space such as an intersection.

impegnino.t: From pegno (a pledge): to commit something, and on the road to commit the vehicle to a space such as an intersection.

impennata.t: From impennarsi, to rear up like a horse, which comes from Spanish empinarse, to stand upright like a pine tree. An impennata is a vehicle rearing up on its back wheel.

impianto.t: From impiantare (to install, to set up), from Latin implantare: something installed and set in place, such as a braking or electrical system.

impiegato.t: Related to the English "employ", which came through French from the same Latin implicare: to put something to use.

impiego.t: Related to the English "employ", which came through French from the same Latin implicare: to put something to use.

importi.t: Not "imports": an importo is an amount of money, a sum. It comes from Italian importare in its sense "to cost, to come to a sum", from Latin importare, to bring in or bring about; English "import" has the same Latin source but took the sense of bringing goods from abroad.

impostare.t: Not "impose" or "impostor": impostare means to set up or lay out something, such as a task, a page or a device like a satellite navigator. It is built on posto, a place, so it means to put each part in its place; English "impose" also began as to put or place, but came to mean to lay a burden on someone.

impostazione.t: Not "imposition": impostazione means a setting, or the way something is laid out or set up. It comes from impostare, to set up or lay out, built from im-, posto and -are; English "imposition" comes instead from Latin impositio, a laying on, and first meant a tax.

imprevedibili.t: Im- (not) plus prevedibile, a relative of prevedere (to foresee), from Latin prae- (before) and videre (to see): unforeseeable.

imprevisti.t: From in- (not) and previsto (foreseen, from pre- and vedere, to see): events that nobody foresaw.

improvvisamente.t: Not "improvised": improvviso means sudden, from Latin improvisus (unforeseen), from in- (not) and provisus (foreseen). English "improvise" came from the Italian verb improvvisare, to perform without preparing, so both words share the idea of something not foreseen.

improvviso.t: Not "improvised": improvviso means sudden, from Latin improvisus (unforeseen), from in- (not) and provisus (foreseen). English "improvise" came from the Italian verb improvvisare, to perform without preparing, so both words share the idea of something not foreseen.

impugnato.t: Not "impugned" here: this impugnare is built on pugno, fist, and means to grip, as with a steering wheel. A separate impugnare, from Latin impugnare, to fight against, does mean to contest, like "impugn". The fist links them, since Latin pugnare, to fight, comes from pugnus, fist.

incamminarsi.t: From cammino (a walk, a way): incamminarsi is to set off on one's way.

incanalamento.t: From canale (channel, canal): to guide vehicles into a channel, as water is guided into a canal.

incanalare.t: From canale (channel, canal): to guide vehicles into a channel, as water is guided into a canal.

incide.t: Not "incise" here: incidere su means to have an effect on something, to weigh on it. This incidere comes from Latin in and cadere, to fall, so it means to fall upon, like English "incident"; "incise" comes from a different Latin verb, built on caedere, to cut.

incidente.t: Like the English "incident" in a traffic report: incidente in these statements means an accident or a crash.

incirca.t: From in plus circa (about): incirca and all'incirca both mean roughly or approximately.

incolonnamento.t: From colonna (column), through incolonnare, to arrange in columns: a line of vehicles one behind another.

incolonnarsi.t: From colonna (column), through incolonnare, to arrange in columns: a line of vehicles one behind another.

incombente.t: Related to the English "incumbent", from Latin incumbere, to lie or lean on. A danger that is incombente hangs over you, just as a duty incumbent on you rests on you.

incrocia.t: From croce (cross): to cross paths with another vehicle, including one coming the other way.

incrociando.t: From croce (cross): to cross paths with another vehicle, including one coming the other way.

incrociano.t: From croce (cross): to cross paths with another vehicle, including one coming the other way.

incrociante.t: From croce (cross): to cross paths with another vehicle, including one coming the other way.

incrociare.t: From croce (cross): to cross paths with another vehicle, including one coming the other way.

indifferentemente.t: Not "indifferently" in the sense of without interest: here indifferentemente means equally, without distinction between the options. Both come from Latin indifferens, not differing; Italian kept the old sense that the choices are alike, while English "indifferent" later came to mean uninterested.

individua.t: Not "individualize" here: individuare means to pinpoint or identify, to single one thing out from others, as a symbol that marks where something is. It is built on individuo (an individual), which goes back to Latin individuus, indivisible, the source of the English "individual"; to individuare something is to pick it out as one single thing.
