individuano.t: Not "individualize" here: individuare means to pinpoint or identify, to single one thing out from others, as a symbol that marks where something is. It is built on individuo (an individual), which goes back to Latin individuus, indivisible, the source of the English "individual"; to individuare something is to pick it out as one single thing.

individuare.t: Not "individualize" here: individuare means to pinpoint or identify, to single one thing out from others, as a symbol that marks where something is. It is built on individuo (an individual), which goes back to Latin individuus, indivisible, the source of the English "individual"; to individuare something is to pick it out as one single thing.

individuazione.t: Not "individuation" here: individuazione means spotting or detection, the act of picking something out. It comes from individuare, built on individuo, an individual, from Latin individuus, indivisible; the Italian verb singles a thing out as one individual, while English "individuation" means making something individual.

indossa.t: From in- and dosso (back, from the Latin dorsum, as in "dorsal"): to put clothing on one's back.

indossando.t: From in- and dosso (back, from the Latin dorsum, as in "dorsal"): to put clothing on one's back.

indossare.t: From in- and dosso (back, from the Latin dorsum, as in "dorsal"): to put clothing on one's back.

indossato.t: From in- and dosso (back, from the Latin dorsum, as in "dorsal"): to put clothing on one's back.

infortunato.t: Not "unfortunate": infortunato means injured, and as a noun an infortunato is an injured person. It is linked to infortunio, from Latin infortunium, misfortune, built on fortuna, luck; Italian narrowed the misfortune to an accident that causes injury, while English "unfortunate" still means unlucky.

infossamento.t: From fossa (a ditch or pit, as in the English "fosse"): sinking into a hollow, as a wheel does in snow or sand.

infuori.t: From in fuori (outward): all'infuori di means everything outside of, so except.

ingorgo.t: Ingorgo comes from ingorgare, to block. Picture traffic caught like water in a gorgo, a whirlpool or eddy.

innestare.t: Innestare is also the gardener's word for grafting one plant onto another; engaging a gear likewise fits one part into another.

inquinamento.t: From Latin inquinare, to stain or befoul, which English kept only in the rare formal word "inquinate". Picture ink spilled into clean water.

inquinano.t: From Latin inquinare, to stain or befoul, which English kept only in the rare formal word "inquinate". Picture ink spilled into clean water.

inquinare.t: From Latin inquinare, to stain or befoul, which English kept only in the rare formal word "inquinate". Picture ink spilled into clean water.

insofferenza.t: Built like the English "insufferable": in- (not) plus a form of soffrire in its sense of to bear. Insofferenza is being unable to bear something, so impatience or annoyance.

integrativo.t: Related to the English "integrate", from Latin integrare (to make whole): integrativo means supplementary, adding what completes something, as a pannello integrativo does.

integrato.t: Related to the English "integrate": integrare here means to supplement or complete, adding what is missing, so integrato means supplemented.

interessa.t: Related to the English "interest": interessare comes from interesse (interest), and here it means to concern or affect, to involve a place or a person.

interessato.t: Related to the English "interest": interessare comes from interesse (interest), and here it means to concern or affect, to involve a place or a person.

intestata.t: From testa (head): a document intestato to someone carries that person's name at its head.

intestatario.t: Compare intestare, to register in someone's name, from testa (head): the intestatario is the holder in whose name a document or vehicle stands.

intralciare.t: From in- plus tralcio, a shoot of a plant. Picture shoots tangled around something and holding it back: intralciare means to hinder or hamper.

intralciato.t: From in- plus tralcio, a shoot of a plant. Picture shoots tangled around something and holding it back: intralciare means to hinder or hamper.

intralcio.t: From in- plus tralcio, a shoot of a plant. Picture shoots tangled around something and holding it back: intralciare means to hinder or hamper.

invalido.t: Related to the English noun "invalid", a person weakened by illness or injury: an invalido is a person with a disability. As an adjective it can also mean void.

invecchiamento.t: From invecchiare, built on vecchio (old): the process of growing old.

inversione.t: Related to the English "inversion", from the same Latin word: an inversione is a reversal, and inversione di marcia is a U-turn, reversing the direction of travel.

investire.t: Besides "invest", investire means to hit or run over someone with a vehicle, which is the sense in these statements.

investirlo.t: Besides "invest", investire means to hit or run over someone with a vehicle, which is the sense in these statements.

investita.t: Besides "invest", investire means to hit or run over someone with a vehicle, which is the sense in these statements.

ippodromo.t: From the Greek hippos (horse, as in "hippopotamus") and dromos (course): a horse-racing track.

irrigidire.t: From rigido (stiff, rigid): to make or become stiff.

lacrimazione.t: From Latin lacrimatio, the flow of tears; the Latin lacrima (tear) also gave the English "lachrymose".

lampeggi.t: From lampo (a flash of lightning), which shares its root with the English "lamp": lampeggiare means to flash on and off.

lampeggiando.t: From lampo (a flash of lightning), which shares its root with the English "lamp": lampeggiare means to flash on and off.

lampeggiano.t: From lampo (a flash of lightning), which shares its root with the English "lamp": lampeggiare means to flash on and off.

lampeggiante.t: From lampo (a flash, as of lightning): lampeggiare is to flash on and off.

lampeggiare.t: From lampo (a flash of lightning), which shares its root with the English "lamp": lampeggiare means to flash on and off.

lampeggio.t: From lampeggiare, itself from lampo (a flash of lightning), which shares its root with the English "lamp": a lampeggio is a flashing on and off.

lanciare.t: Related to the English "launch" and "lance": lanciare means to throw or hurl.

larga.t: Not "large" here: largo means wide, the opposite of stretto (narrow). Both come from Latin largus, abundant; Italian uses it for width, as Old French did with "broad, wide", while English "large" settled on size in general.

larghezza.t: Not "largeness": larghezza means width, from largo (wide). Largo and the English "large" both come from Latin largus, abundant or generous; the English word came to mean big in general, while Italian largo settled on wide.

larghi.t: Not "large" here: largo means wide, the opposite of stretto (narrow). Both come from Latin largus, abundant; Italian uses it for width, as Old French did with "broad, wide", while English "large" settled on size in general.

lavacristallo.t: From lavare (to wash, as in "lavatory") and cristallo (glass): the device that washes the windshield.

lavaggio.t: From the French lavage, from laver (to wash); the English "lavatory" also goes back to a Latin word for washing.

lega.t: From legare (to bind), from Latin ligare, which also gave the English "ligament": a lega is an alloy, metals fused into one.

legati.t: From legare (to tie or bind), the same root as the English "ligament" and "obligate".

lesione.t: Related to the English "lesion", both from Latin laesio (a hurting): lesione is the general word for damage or a bodily injury, as in lesioni personali.

lettura.t: Not a "lecture" here: lettura means reading, from leggere, to read, though it can also mean a lecture. Both come from Late Latin lectura, a reading; English "lecture" began as a reading aloud to students and came to mean the talk itself, while Italian kept the plain act of reading.

libretto.t: The English "libretto", the words of an opera, is borrowed from this Italian word for a little book: here libretto means a booklet, such as a vehicle's registration document.

lieve.t: From Latin levis (light), the root of the English "levity" and "alleviate": lieve means light or slight.

limitrofa.t: From Late Latin limitrophus, built on limes (boundary), the source of the English "limit": limitrofo means bordering or adjacent.

longherone.t: From the French longeron, linked to long (long): a longherone is a beam that runs lengthwise, such as the side beams of a vehicle frame.

macchie.t: From Latin macula (spot), the root of the English "immaculate" (spotless): a macchia is a stain or spot.

maggiorenne.t: Built on maggiore (greater), as in maggiore età, the age of majority: a maggiorenne is someone who has come of age.

malessere.t: Also written mal essere, it is the opposite of benessere (well-being): a vague feeling of being unwell.

manomesse.t: From Latin manumittere (to free a slave), later read as mettere mano (to put a hand on): today it means to tamper with something.

manomissione.t: From Latin manumittere (to free a slave), later read as mettere mano (to put a hand on): today it means to tamper with something.

manubrio.t: From Latin manubrium, built on manus (hand): the handlebar is the part the hands grip.

manutenzione.t: From Latin manu tenere (to hold in the hand), the same root as the English "maintenance".

marce.t: Not "marches" here: marce, the plural of marcia, are the gears of a vehicle. Marcia comes from marciare, to march, and Italian stretched it from marching to any forward movement of a vehicle and then to each gear ratio of the gearbox.

marcia.t: Related to the English "march": marcia here is the forward movement of a vehicle, as in senso di marcia, the direction of travel.

marciando.t: Related to the English "march": both come from French marcher, and said of a vehicle, marciare means to travel or move along a road.

marciano.t: Related to the English "march": both come from French marcher, and said of a vehicle, marciare means to travel or move along a road.

marciapiede.t: From the French marchepied, made of marcher (to walk) and pied (foot): the part of the street kept for people on foot.

marciare.t: Related to the English "march": both come from French marcher, and said of a vehicle, marciare means to travel or move along a road.

marciarvi.t: Related to the English "march": both come from French marcher, and said of a vehicle, marciare means to travel or move along a road.

mareggiata.t: Built on mare (sea), through mareggiare: storm waves, driven by strong wind, that break violently against the shore.

marmitta.t: Originally a cooking pot, from the French marmite; the name passed to the car's muffler.

mascherare.t: From maschera (mask): mascherare means to mask, that is, to hide or cover.

mascherina.t: A diminutive of maschera (mask): a small mask or cover, such as the grille over a radiator.

massi.t: Related to massa, the Italian word for "mass": a masso is a boulder, a large mass of rock, as in caduta massi (falling rocks).

massimale.t: As an adjective massimale means "maximal"; as a noun, a massimale is a maximum limit, such as the most an insurance policy will pay.

mastice.t: Like the English "mastic", it comes from the Greek name of a tree resin; today mastice is a paste or glue used to seal and bond.

mediante.t: From the medieval Latin mediante, from mediare (to be in the middle): mediante means by means of or with the help of.

medicare.t: Related to the English "medicate", both from Latin medicare: medicare means to dress a wound or treat an injured person.

merci.t: From Latin merx (goods), which is also inside the English "commerce": merci are goods, such as those carried as freight.

mescolano.t: From Vulgar Latin misculare, built on Latin miscere (to mix): mescolare means to mix or blend.

mezzeria.t: From mezzo (middle): the mezzeria is the line that divides the carriageway down the middle, lengthwise.

mezzo.t: Besides "half" or "middle", as in mezzo-soprano, mezzo means a means of doing something, and a vehicle, as in mezzi pubblici.

minacciati.t: Related to the English "menace": minacciare means to threaten.

minorenni.t: Built on minore (lesser), the opposite of maggiorenne: a minorenne is someone who has not yet come of age.

molle.t: Molla means a spring; it comes from mollare (to let go, to slacken), itself from molle (soft, yielding).

molo.t: Related to the English "mole", a stone pier or breakwater: molo means a pier or dock.

monoposto.t: From mono- (one) and posto (seat): a vehicle with a single seat.

motrice.t: Short for macchina motrice and related to motore (engine): the motrice is the powered unit that pulls the vehicles hitched behind it.

mozziconi.t: Related to mozzicare: a mozzicone is the stub left of something burned, cut or used up, such as a cigarette butt.

munito.t: From Latin munire (to fortify), the root of the English "munitions": munito means equipped or provided with.

muretti.t: A diminutive of muro (wall, as in "mural"): a muretto is a low wall.

nebbia.t: From Latin nebula (mist, cloud), the root of the English "nebula" and "nebulous": nebbia means fog.

neopatentato.t: From neo- and patentato (licensed, from patente): a driver who has only recently obtained the license.

netto.t: Not "net" as in net weight here: netto also means clear. It goes back to Latin nitidus, shining, which also gave English "neat"; the "net" of net weight belongs to the same family and means clear of anything extra.

noiosa.t: Not "noisy": noioso means boring or tedious, and it can also mean annoying. It comes from noia, which goes back, probably through Old Occitan, to the Latin phrase in odio (hateful), the same source as the English "annoy" and "ennui".

nonché.t: Built from non and che, literally "not that": nonché means as well as or and also.

nonostante.t: From non and ostante (standing in the way, from Latin obstare, as in "obstacle"): with nothing in the way, that is, despite.

notevole.t: Built on notare (to note), notevole can mean "notable", and in these statements it means considerable, large in amount or degree.

notevolmente.t: Close to the English "notably" in "notably faster": notevolmente, from notevole, means considerably, to a large degree.

occorre.t: Not "occur" in everyday use: occorre means it is necessary, or one needs; to happen is only a literary sense. Both come from Latin occurrere, to run to meet, from ob, toward, and currere, to run; English followed the sense "to present itself" to "to happen", while everyday Italian now uses it for what is needed.

occorrendo.t: Not "occur" in everyday use: occorre means it is necessary, or one needs; to happen is only a literary sense. Both come from Latin occurrere, to run to meet, from ob, toward, and currere, to run; English followed the sense "to present itself" to "to happen", while everyday Italian now uses it for what is needed.

occorrerà.t: Not "occur" in everyday use: occorre means it is necessary, or one needs; to happen is only a literary sense. Both come from Latin occurrere, to run to meet, from ob, toward, and currere, to run; English followed the sense "to present itself" to "to happen", while everyday Italian now uses it for what is needed.

occorrono.t: Not "occur" in everyday use: occorre means it is necessary, or one needs; to happen is only a literary sense. Both come from Latin occurrere, to run to meet, from ob, toward, and currere, to run; English followed the sense "to present itself" to "to happen", while everyday Italian now uses it for what is needed.

occulta.t: Related to the English "occult", which first meant hidden or secret: occultare, from Latin occultare, means to hide from view.

officina.t: Not "office": an officina is a workshop, and an officina meccanica is a garage that repairs vehicles. Both words go back to Latin opus, work, and facere, to make or do; officina named the place where things are made, while "office" comes from officium, a duty or service, and only later meant a room for business.

oltrepassando.t: From oltre (beyond) and passare (to pass): to pass beyond a point or line.

oltrepassandolo.t: From oltre (beyond) and passare (to pass): to pass beyond a point or line.

oltrepassata.t: From oltre (beyond) and passare (to pass): to pass beyond a point or line.

oltrepassi.t: From oltre (beyond) and passare (to pass): to pass beyond a point or line.

omologato.t: From Medieval Latin homologare, from Greek homologos (corresponding): omologato means officially recognized as meeting set standards, as a prototype is once it has been tested.

omologazione.t: From Medieval Latin homologare, from Greek homologos (corresponding): omologato means officially recognized as meeting set standards, as a prototype is once it has been tested.

operai.t: From opera (work), the root of the English "operate": an operaio is a manual worker.

opere.t: Opere is the plural of opera, a work, so opere stradali are road works. The English "opera" was borrowed from this same Italian word.

oppone.t: Related to the English "oppose": both go back to Latin opponere, to set against, from ob- (in the way) and ponere (to put). Si oppone means it sets itself against, so grip si oppone allo slittamento when it resists the slide.

opportunamente.t: From opportuno, which means "opportune" or suitable: opportunamente means suitably, in the way the situation requires.

opportuno.t: Like the English "opportune" (fitting, well timed): è opportuno means it is advisable, the right thing to do.

organi.t: Like the English "organ", a part of a body that does a job: organi here are the working parts of a machine or vehicle.

osso.t: Related to the English "ossify": both come from the Latin os, ossis (bone).

ove.t: An old, formal form of dove (where), from the Latin ubi.

paletta.t: A diminutive of pala (shovel, blade): a paletta is a small paddle held up by hand.

palpebra.t: Kept almost unchanged from the Latin palpebra (eyelid).

panno.t: From the Latin pannus: a panno is a piece of cloth, such as one used for cleaning.

parabrezza.t: From para- and brezza (breeze), modeled on the French pare-brise: the glass that keeps the wind off.

pari.t: From the Latin par (genitive paris), meaning equal, as in pari a, equal to.

pascolo.t: From the Latin pascuum, built on pascere (to graze): a pascolo is land where livestock graze.

passeggino.t: From passeggio (a walk): a passeggino is the small wheeled seat for taking a child out for a walk.

pastiglie.t: Besides a "pastille" or lozenge, pastiglie are brake pads, short for pastiglie dei freni.

pattinare.t: From the French patiner, built on patin (a skate, Italian pattino): a wheel that pattina slips as a skate does instead of gripping.

pecuniario.t: From the Latin pecuniarius, built on pecunia (money): pecuniario means having to do with money.

pedivella.t: Modeled on manovella, with piede (foot) put in place of mano (hand): a crank or lever worked by the foot.

pedone.t: Built on the Latin pes, pedis (foot): a pedone is someone who goes on foot.

pendenza.t: From pendere: pendenza is the lean or slope of a road or surface.

pene.t: The plural of pena, a penalty or punishment, from the Latin poena.

penzolante.t: From penzolare (to dangle), probably from a Latin form built on pendere (to hang): something penzolante hangs and swings loosely.

percorre.t: From per (through) and correre (to run): to run through, to travel the length of a road. Percorso is the route covered.

percorrendo.t: From per (through) and correre (to run): to run through, to travel the length of a road. Percorso is the route covered.

percorrere.t: From per (through) and correre (to run): to run through, to travel the length of a road. Percorso is the route covered.

percorribile.t: From per (through) and correre (to run): to run through, to travel the length of a road. Percorso is the route covered.

percorrono.t: From per (through) and correre (to run): to run through, to travel the length of a road. Percorso is the route covered.

percorso.t: From per (through) and correre (to run): to run through, to travel the length of a road. Percorso is the route covered.

personale.t: Not "personal" when it is a noun: il personale means the staff, the English "personnel". As an adjective it does mean personal. The noun comes from French personnel, the adjective used as a noun, which is exactly where English "personnel" comes from too.

pertanto.t: From per and tanto, here meaning that: for that reason, therefore.

pianeggiante.t: From pianeggiare, built on piano (flat, level): pianeggiante describes ground or a road without noticeable slopes.

piazzola.t: A diminutive of piazza: a small open space, here a paved area beside the road.

piegate.t: From the Latin plicare: piegare means to bend or to fold.

pietrisco.t: From pietra (stone): a mass of small broken stones.

pneumatico.t: Like the English "pneumatic" (worked by air), pneumatico comes from Greek pneuma, air or breath: as a noun, il pneumatico is a tire.

poggiatesta.t: From poggiare (to rest on) and testa (head): the support the head rests against.

poggiato.t: From a Latin verb built on podium (a pedestal): poggiare means to rest one thing on another.

polizza.t: The source of the English insurance "policy", which came into English through French from this Italian word.

polso.t: From the Latin pulsus (a beat): the wrist is where the pulse is felt, and polso also means the pulse itself.

polvere.t: From the Latin pulvis (genitive pulveris): polvere is dust or any fine powder.

ponendosi.t: From porre (to put, to place), from the Latin ponere: ponendosi means placing itself.

pontile.t: From ponte (bridge): a walkway built out over the water, like a short bridge.

portapacchi.t: From porta (carries) and pacchi (packages): a rack on a vehicle that holds loads being carried.

portata.t: From portare (to carry): the portata of a vehicle is how much it is able to carry.

portiera.t: From porta (door): a portiera is the door of a vehicle.

possibilmente.t: Not "possibly" in the sense of perhaps: possibilmente means if possible. It is possibile plus the adverb ending -mente, and possibile comes from Latin possibilis, from posse (to be able), so read it as "if one can".

posta.t: Not "mail" here: posta is the feminine of posto, the past participle of porre, so it means placed or located. Porre comes from Latin ponere, to place, and the English "post" of mail grew from the same idea: riders and horses were placed at intervals along a route.

poste.t: Not "mail" here: posta is the feminine of posto, the past participle of porre, so it means placed or located. Porre comes from Latin ponere, to place, and the English "post" of mail grew from the same idea: riders and horses were placed at intervals along a route.

posteggiare.t: Built on posto (a place, a spot): posteggiare means to put a vehicle in its spot, the same as parcheggiare.

posteggiato.t: Built on posto (a place, a spot): posteggiare means to put a vehicle in its spot, the same as parcheggiare.

posteggio.t: Built on posto (a place, a spot): posteggiare means to put a vehicle in its spot, the same as parcheggiare.

pozzanghere.t: Built on pozza (a small pool of standing water), a relative of pozzo (a well).

preavvisa.t: From pre- (before) and avvisare (to warn, to notify): to give notice ahead of time.

preavvisare.t: From pre- (before) and avvisare (to warn), which shares its root with the English "advise": to warn ahead of time.

preavviso.t: From pre- (before) and avviso (notice), which shares its root with the English "advice": a notice given ahead of time.

precisa.t: Built on preciso, the Italian for "precise": precisare is a verb meaning to specify or state exactly, that is, to make something precise.

precisare.t: Built on preciso, the Italian for "precise": precisare is a verb meaning to specify or state exactly, that is, to make something precise.

precoce.t: From Latin praecox, ripened early, from prae (before) and coquere (to ripen, literally to cook). English "precocious" first described fruit ripe before its time and later a child mature before their time; precoce means early or premature in the same way, so usura precoce is wear that comes before its time.

predisporsi.t: Predisporsi means to get ready in advance, from pre- (before) and disporre (to arrange), rather than "predispose" in the sense of inclining someone.

predisposte.t: Predisposto means set up or arranged in advance for a purpose, from pre- (before) and disporre (to arrange), rather than "predisposed" in the sense of inclined.

pregiudica.t: Not "prejudice" in the sense of bias: pregiudicare usually means to compromise or endanger. Both come from Latin praeiudicare, to judge beforehand; Italian moved from a judgment given too early to the harm it does, and English keeps that harm mainly as a legal sense, while everyday English uses the word for bias.

premendo.t: From the Latin premere: to press, push down, or put pressure on.

premere.t: From the Latin premere: to press, push down, or put pressure on.

preposto.t: The past participle of preporre, from the Latin praepositus: the person or office placed in charge of a task.

prescrizione.t: Like the English "prescription", something laid down to be followed: in these statements a prescrizione is a rule or regulation that requires or forbids something.

presegnala.t: From pre- (before) and segnalare (to signal): to signal something ahead of time.

presegnalare.t: From pre- (before) and segnalare (to signal): to signal something ahead of time.

presegnalazione.t: From presegnalare (to signal ahead): a presegnalazione is an advance warning, such as a panel announcing a hazard farther on.

presso.t: From Latin presse (narrow, short) and a cousin of the French près: presso means near, beside, or at a place.

prestare.t: Prestare means to lend; prestare attenzione is to lend one's attention and prestare soccorso to lend aid, much as English says "lend a hand".

prestato.t: Prestare means to lend; prestare attenzione is to lend one's attention and prestare soccorso to lend aid, much as English says "lend a hand".

prestazioni.t: From prestare (to lend or provide): what a machine or a person provides, hence its performance.

pretendere.t: Not "pretend" in the sense of make-believe: pretendere means to demand, or to expect something as a right. Both come from Latin praetendere, to stretch out in front or put forward; Italian kept "to put forward a claim", while English "pretend" came to mean putting forward a false show.

prevede.t: From pre- (before) and vedere (to see): to foresee. A law that prevede something has foreseen it, and so provides for it.

prevedere.t: From pre- (before) and vedere (to see): to foresee. A law that prevede something has foreseen it, and so provides for it.

previsto.t: From prevedere (to foresee): something previsto has been foreseen, hence provided for or scheduled.

principiante.t: From principiare (to begin), related to principio (start): a principiante is someone at the start. The English "principle" shares the Latin root principium.

privi.t: Privo di means lacking or without, related to the English "privation" and "deprivation".

procurato.t: Not "procured" in the sense of obtained: procurare here means to cause or bring about, as in procurare un danno. Both come from Latin procurare, to take care of or manage; English "procure" also meant to bring about or cause at first, and only later settled on obtaining.

progettate.t: Not "projected": progettare means to design or plan, like drawing up a project. English "project" goes back to Latin proicere, to throw forward, the notion being to cast a plan forward in the mind; Italian took progettare from French projeter and kept that planning sense, while English "projected" now usually means forecast.

proiettati.t: Like the English "project" in its sense of throwing forward, as with a projectile: proiettare means to cast or throw, so proiettati means thrown or hurled.

proiettore.t: Like the English "projector", a device that throws light forward: in a vehicle the proiettore is the headlight unit.

proprio.t: Not "proper" in the everyday sense: proprio means one's own, and as an adverb it means exactly or really. Both come from Latin proprius, one's own, the root of English "property"; English "proper" drifted toward correct or fitting, keeping the old sense in "proper name", while Italian kept one's own as its main sense.

proseguimento.t: From proseguire (to continue), which comes from Latin prosequi (to follow onward), the source of the English "pursue": a continuation.

proseguire.t: Related to the English "pursue" and "prosecute": all come from Latin prosequi (to follow onward). Proseguire is to go on, to continue.

protrae.t: Related to the English "protracted": both come from Latin protrahere. Something that si protrae is prolonged, so it drags on in time.

protrarsi.t: Related to the English "protracted": both come from Latin protrahere. Something that si protrae is prolonged, so it drags on in time.

provenendo.t: From Latin provenire (to come forth), which is also the source of the English "provenance": provenire means to come from a place or to originate.

provenga.t: From Latin provenire (to come forth), which is also the source of the English "provenance": provenire means to come from a place or to originate.

provengano.t: From Latin provenire (to come forth), which is also the source of the English "provenance": provenire means to come from a place or to originate.

provengono.t: From Latin provenire (to come forth), which is also the source of the English "provenance": provenire means to come from a place or to originate.

provenienti.t: From Latin provenire (to come forth), which is also the source of the English "provenance": provenire means to come from a place or to originate.

provenire.t: From Latin provenire (to come forth), which is also the source of the English "provenance": provenire means to come from a place or to originate.

proviene.t: From Latin provenire (to come forth), which is also the source of the English "provenance": provenire means to come from a place or to originate.

provoca.t: Like the English "provoke" in "provoke a reaction": provocare means to cause or bring about, and it can also mean to provoke someone.

provocandone.t: Like the English "provoke" in "provoke a reaction": provocare means to cause or bring about, and it can also mean to provoke someone.

provocano.t: Like the English "provoke" in "provoke a reaction": provocare means to cause or bring about, and it can also mean to provoke someone.

provocare.t: Like the English "provoke" in "provoke a reaction": provocare means to cause or bring about, and it can also mean to provoke someone.

provocarne.t: Like the English "provoke" in "provoke a reaction": provocare means to cause or bring about, and it can also mean to provoke someone.

provocato.t: Like the English "provoke" in "provoke a reaction": provocare means to cause or bring about, and it can also mean to provoke someone.

provochi.t: Like the English "provoke" in "provoke a reaction": provocare means to cause or bring about, and it can also mean to provoke someone.

provvedere.t: Related to the English "provide", since both come from Latin providere: provvedere means to see to something, to take the necessary steps or arrange for it.

provvederà.t: Related to the English "provide", since both come from Latin providere: provvedere means to see to something, to take the necessary steps or arrange for it.

provvisto.t: The past participle of provvedere: provvisto di means supplied or equipped with, close to the English "provided with".

psichici.t: Not "psychic" in the sense of reading minds: psichico means relating to the mind, that is, mental or psychological. Both come from Greek psykhikos, of the soul or mind; Italian kept that plain sense, while English "psychic" also took on the sense of mind reading and second sight.

pulsante.t: Built on pulsare and modeled on the French poussoir, from pousser (to push): the pulsante is the part you press to make a device work.

punte.t: Punta is a pointed tip or end, from late Latin puncta, built on pungere (to prick).

punteggio.t: Built on punto (point): the total of points, a score.

pur.t: A short form of pure (also, even): pur with a gerund means even while or even though.

purché.t: Made of pur (only) and che (that): only on the condition that, provided that.

quadro.t: Quadro first means a square, from Latin quadrum (a square figure); it also names a panel of instruments and controls, as in a car.

quintali.t: A quintale is a hundred kilograms; the word came through Spanish from the Arabic qintar and goes back to a Latin word linked to a hundred.

raddoppia.t: Built on doppio (double): to make double.

raddoppiata.t: Built on doppio (double): to make double.

raffigurato.t: Built on figura (figure, picture): to show in a figure or picture.

rafforza.t: Built on forza (strength, force): to make stronger, to reinforce.

raffreddamento.t: Built on freddo (cold): making cold, hence cooling.

raffreddi.t: Built on freddo (cold): raffreddarsi is to become cold.

raggio.t: Raggio means a ray, and also the radius of a circle; both senses come from Latin radius.

rallenta.t: Built on lento (slow): to make slower, to slow down.

rallentamento.t: Built on lento (slow): a slowing down.

rallentando.t: Built on lento (slow): to make slower, to slow down.

rallentano.t: Built on lento (slow): to make slower, to slow down.

rallentare.t: Built on lento (slow): to make slower, to slow down.

rallentato.t: Built on lento (slow): to make slower, to slow down.

rapporto.t: Not "rapport": here rapporto means a ratio, or a relationship between two things. It can also mean a report, but not in these statements. English borrowed "rapport" from French in the broad sense of relation and later narrowed it to a harmonious understanding between people, while Italian rapporto kept the broad sense.

razze.t: Picture the spokes radiating from the hub of a steering wheel: here razza means a spoke, not a breed.

rca.t: Short for responsabilità civile autoveicoli: civil liability for motor vehicles.

realizzata.t: Here realizzare means to make real, that is, to build or carry out, rather than "realize" in the sense of understand.

reato.t: From late Latin reatus, the state of being accused, built on reus (the accused): a reato is a crime punishable under the law.

recanti.t: From recare (to carry or bring): recante means bearing or carrying, as a sign bears a symbol.

recintato.t: From recinto (an enclosed space), the past participle of recingere: recintare is to surround a place with a fence or wall.

regolarmente.t: Like "regularly" in part, but regolarmente often means properly or duly, in accordance with the rules.

regolarsi.t: Regolarsi is to regulate oneself: to adjust one's behavior to the situation.

relative.t: Not "relative" as a family member or as comparative: here relative means the related ones, those that go with the thing just named, such as the documents for an application. Both come from Late Latin relativus, having reference to something, from referre, to carry back; the English phrase "relative to" still carries that first sense.

rendano.t: Related to the English "render", as in "render useless": rendere means to make, as in rendere difficile, to make difficult.

rende.t: Related to the English "render", as in "render useless": rendere means to make, as in rendere difficile, to make difficult.

rendere.t: Related to the English "render", as in "render useless": rendere means to make, as in rendere difficile, to make difficult.

rendersi.t: Related to the English "render", as in "render useless": rendere means to make, as in rendere difficile, to make difficult.

rendimento.t: From rendere (to give back, yield): what a machine gives back, its efficiency or output.

rendono.t: Related to the English "render", as in "render useless": rendere means to make, as in rendere difficile, to make difficult.

restituiti.t: From Latin restituere, to put back in its former place: restituire means to give back.

restringimento.t: From restringere (to narrow), the same Latin word that gave the English "restrict": a narrowing.

retro.t: Not "retro" in the sense of old-fashioned: retro means the back or rear, from Latin retro, behind. English "retro" came from French, short for rétrograde, going backward, so it points back in time, while the Italian word points to the back side of a thing.

retrocedere.t: From Latin retrocedere, made of retro (backward) and cedere (to go): to go backward.

retromarcia.t: Made of retro (backward) and marcia: driving a vehicle backward, and also the gear that does it.

rettilineo.t: From late Latin rectilineus, made of rectus (straight) and linea (line): a rettilineo is a straight stretch of road.

revisione.t: Here revisione is the official inspection of a vehicle, or the retest of a license holder, rather than the "revision" of a text.

rialzato.t: Built on alzare (to raise), with ri-: raised up.

ribaltamento.t: Picture a table flipped over: ribaltare is to tip over or overturn, and ribaltamento is the overturning.

richiamare.t: From ri- (again) and chiamare (to call): to call back, or to call attention to something.

richiede.t: From Latin requirere: richiedere means to ask for or request something, and so to require it.

richiedente.t: From richiedere (to request): the person making a request, the applicant.

ricorrere.t: Ricorrere a means to turn to or resort to someone or something, a sense "recur" does not carry. Its literal sense is to run back.

rifornimento.t: From ri- (again) and fornire (to supply, the same root as the English "furnish"): supplying the vehicle again, that is, refueling.

riga.t: Riga means a line, and it can also mean a ruler; the smaller word for a ruler, righello, is built on it.

rigata.t: From riga (line): a surface that is rigata has lines drawn across it, that is, it is scratched.

rilasciare.t: When the object is a document, rilasciare means to issue it, as an office issues a license or a certificate, rather than to "release" it.

rilasciato.t: When the object is a document, rilasciare means to issue it, as an office issues a license or a certificate, rather than to "release" it.

rilascio.t: For a document, rilascio is its issuing, as of a license or a certificate, rather than a "release". The verb is rilasciare, to issue.

rilevamento.t: From rilevare (to notice or detect): rilevamento is the act of detecting or surveying something, as a sensor or a survey does.

rimorchi.t: Related to rimorchiare (to tow): a rimorchio is a tow, and also the towed vehicle, a trailer.

rimorchio.t: Related to rimorchiare (to tow): a rimorchio is a tow, and also the towed vehicle, a trailer.

riparo.t: Not "repair": riparo means a shelter. It comes from riparare, which goes back to Latin reparare, the source of English "repair", and in Italian that verb means to protect or shelter as well as to fix. Riparo keeps the sheltering sense.

ripartendo.t: From ri- and partire: ripartire means to leave or start again. A second verb with the same spelling means to divide up or distribute, as a load is distributed.

ripartire.t: From ri- and partire: ripartire means to leave or start again. A second verb with the same spelling means to divide up or distribute, as a load is distributed.

ripartito.t: From ri- and partire: ripartire means to leave or start again. A second verb with the same spelling means to divide up or distribute, as a load is distributed.

ripida.t: An altered form of rapido (fast), shaped by ripa (shore or bank): picture a road as steep as the face of a high bank.

ripiegata.t: From ri- and piegare (to fold or bend), which comes from Latin plicare; the English "pliable" goes back to the same ancient root.

riporta.t: Related to the English "report", both from Latin reportare, to carry back: riportare here means to show or bear written text, as a sign bears place names.

riportata.t: Related to the English "report", both from Latin reportare, to carry back: riportare here means to show or bear written text, as a sign bears place names.

riposto.t: From riporre (to put back or put away), which comes from Latin reponere and is built from ri- and porre: riposto means put away, stored.

ripresa.t: Ripresa means a resumption or a recovery; said of a car, it is the pickup, the acceleration when moving off again.

ripristinare.t: From ri- and pristino (original, as in the English "pristine"): to bring something back to its original state, that is, to restore it.

riquadro.t: Built from ri- and quadro: a riquadro is a square or four-sided section of a surface, such as a box or panel within a sign.

risalire.t: From ri- and salire (to go up): to go back up, and so to trace something back to its source, such as a plate back to its owner.

risarcimento.t: From Latin resarcire, to patch or mend again: risarcire means to make good a loss by paying for it, and risarcimento is that payment.

risarcisce.t: From Latin resarcire, to patch or mend again: risarcire means to make good a loss by paying for it, and risarcimento is that payment.

risarcito.t: From Latin resarcire, to patch or mend again: risarcire means to make good a loss by paying for it, and risarcimento is that payment.

riscuote.t: Built on scuotere (to shake): riscuotere means to collect money that is owed, as an insurer collects premiums.

risparmiando.t: From a Germanic root shared with the English "spare": risparmiare means to save or to spare, as in sparing fuel.

risparmiare.t: From a Germanic root shared with the English "spare": risparmiare means to save or to spare, as in sparing fuel.

ristrettezza.t: Built on ristretto (restricted or limited), from Latin restrictus: ristrettezza is the state of being restricted, as in a tight space.

ritenendo.t: Not "retain" here: in these statements ritenere means to believe or consider, as in ritengo che, I believe that. Both come from Latin retinere, to hold back, from re- and tenere (to hold); Italian also uses the verb for holding an opinion, much as English says "I hold that".

ritenga.t: Not "retain" here: in these statements ritenere means to believe or consider, as in ritengo che, I believe that. Both come from Latin retinere, to hold back, from re- and tenere (to hold); Italian also uses the verb for holding an opinion, much as English says "I hold that".

ritiene.t: Not "retain" here: in these statements ritenere means to believe or consider, as in ritengo che, I believe that. Both come from Latin retinere, to hold back, from re- and tenere (to hold); Italian also uses the verb for holding an opinion, much as English says "I hold that".

ritiro.t: Not "retirement" here: ritiro means a withdrawal, a collection, or a confiscation, as when a license is taken away. It comes from ritirare, from ri-, back, and tirare, to pull, so it is literally a pulling back; English "retire" has the same make-up through French retirer, to draw back, and only later came to mean leaving one's work.

rivenditore.t: Built on rivendere (to resell): a rivenditore is someone who resells goods to the public, that is, a retailer or dealer.

rivolgersi.t: From rivolgere, which comes from Latin revolvere, the same source as the English "revolve": rivolgersi a means to turn to someone for help.

rivolto.t: From rivolgere (to turn toward), the same Latin root as "revolve": rivolto means turned toward, directed at or addressed to.

rotaie.t: Built on rota, an old form of ruota (wheel), from Latin rota: the rotaie are the rails that the wheels of a tram or train run on. Do not confuse it with rotatoria, a roundabout: both words are built on the word for wheel, which is why they look alike.

rottamare.t: From rottame (scrap or wreckage), which comes from rotto (broken): to rottamare a vehicle is to turn it into scrap.

rottamarlo.t: From rottame (scrap or wreckage), which comes from rotto (broken): to rottamare a vehicle is to turn it into scrap.

rottura.t: From the Latin ruptura, built on rumpere (to break), which also gave rompere. The English "rupture" comes from the same Latin word.

roulotte.t: A French word, from rouler (to roll): a trailer that a car tows, fitted out for living in, especially at campsites.

rovesciamenti.t: From rovesciare (to overturn or spill), from the same Latin root as the English "reverse": turning something upside down.

ruggine.t: From the Latin aerugo, the green rust that forms on copper: ruggine is the red-brown rust on iron.

rugoso.t: From ruga (wrinkle), the root of the English "corrugated": a surface full of small ridges, that is, rough.

rumore.t: Not "rumor" here: rumore means noise, any sound, such as that of an engine or a horn. Both come from Latin rumor, which meant both noise and common talk; Italian kept the noise, while English kept the talk.

rumorosi.t: Not about rumors: rumoroso means noisy, from rumore (noise). Rumore and English "rumor" both come from Latin rumor, which meant noise as well as common talk; Italian kept the noise, while English kept the talk.

rumorosità.t: Not about rumors: rumorosità is the noise level, from rumoroso (noisy). Rumore and the English "rumor" both come from Latin rumor, noise or common talk; Italian kept the noise, while English kept the talk.

ruotino.t: From ruota (wheel) with the small ending -ino: a little wheel. Alone it usually means the narrow spare wheel carried for emergencies, but in ruotino pivottante di manovra it is the small swiveling wheel under a trailer's nose.

ruvido.t: From the Latin rugidus, built on ruga (wrinkle): a ruvido surface is rough and coarse. Said of manners, it can also mean rude.

sagoma.t: Picture a cardboard cutout of a person: that flat outline is a sagoma, the shape or profile of an object.

saldamente.t: From saldo (firm, steady), which probably goes back to the Latin solidus, the source of the English "solid": firmly.

saldatura.t: From saldare (to join firmly or weld), built on saldo (firm). The English "solder" comes from the Latin solidus (solid), which is probably also behind saldo.

saltellamenti.t: From saltellare (to hop, making small quick jumps), a derivative of saltare (to jump), which comes from the Latin saltare.

salvagente.t: From salvare (to save) and gente (people): a thing that keeps people safe, here a raised island where pedestrians wait.

salvo.t: Like the old English "save" in "all save one": salvo means except or unless. Both come from the Latin salvus (safe).

sanguinamento.t: From sanguinare (to bleed), built on sangue (blood). The English "sanguine" comes from the Latin sanguis (blood), the source of sangue.

sbandamenti.t: Not "abandonment": sbandare is built on banda (side), also the word for each side of a ship, so it means to veer or skid to one side, or for a ship to list. "Abandon" comes instead through Old French à bandon, "at will", from a Germanic word meaning to proclaim, so the two only look alike.

sbandi.t: Not "abandonment": sbandare is built on banda (side), also the word for each side of a ship, so it means to veer or skid to one side, or for a ship to list. "Abandon" comes instead through Old French à bandon, "at will", from a Germanic word meaning to proclaim, so the two only look alike.

sbarrata.t: From s- and barra (bar), as in the English "bar" and "barrier": closed off by a bar.

sbarre.t: Related to the English "bar": the sbarre are the bars that drop across the road at a crossing.

sbocchi.t: From sboccare, built on bocca (mouth) with the prefix s-: the place where one road comes out onto another.

sbocco.t: From sboccare, built on bocca (mouth) with the prefix s-: the place where one road comes out onto another.

sbrinare.t: From brina (frost) with the prefix s-: to take the frost off, that is, to defrost.

scada.t: From the Latin excadere, built on cadere (to fall): a deadline falls due and passes, so scadere means to expire.

scaduto.t: From the Latin excadere, built on cadere (to fall): a deadline falls due and passes, so scadere means to expire.

scalzamenti.t: From scalzare, from the Latin excalceare, built on calceus (shoe): scalzarsi means to take off one's shoes, and scalzamenti are shoes slipping off the foot.

scalzarsi.t: From scalzare, from the Latin excalceare, built on calceus (shoe): scalzarsi means to take off one's shoes, and scalzamenti are shoes slipping off the foot.

scarico.t: From scaricare (to unload), which is caricare (to load) with the prefix s-: unloading, and the tubo di scarico that discharges the exhaust.

scattata.t: Picture the snap of a spring-loaded trap: scattare means to spring into action or be triggered, as a light switches on.

schiaffi.t: Sounds like the noise it describes: a schiaffo is a slap.

schienale.t: From schiena (back): the schienale is the part of a seat that supports the back.

schivare.t: From a Germanic root shared with the English "eschew": schivare means to avoid something by moving aside, to dodge.

scivolamento.t: Picture a ski (sci in Italian) gliding over snow: scivolare is to slide or slip, and a scivolamento is a slide or skid.

scivolando.t: Picture a ski (sci in Italian) gliding over snow: scivolare is to slide or slip, and a scivolamento is a slide or skid.

scivolare.t: Picture a ski (sci in Italian) gliding over snow: scivolare is to slide or slip, and a scivolamento is a slide or skid.

scivoloso.t: Picture a ski (sci in Italian) gliding over snow: scivoloso means slippery, a surface on which things slide easily.

scolaro.t: Not "scholar": scolaro means a schoolchild or pupil, and it is related to scuola, school. Both come from Medieval Latin scholaris, a pupil, from schola, school; English "scholar" also first meant a pupil, but its sense of a learned person is the one that now prevails.

scongiurare.t: Related to the English "conjure": both come from the Latin coniurare, and scongiurare means to avert or ward off a danger.

sconnessioni.t: On a road surface, sconnessioni are gaps and uneven patches where the pieces no longer join, a narrower sense than "disconnection".

sconsigliabile.t: Sconsigliabile means not advisable: the opposite of consigliabile, something one would advise against.

sconsigliata.t: Sconsigliabile means not advisable: the opposite of consigliabile, something one would advise against.

scopo.t: Not "scope": scopo means purpose or aim. English "scope" was borrowed from this Italian word, which goes back through Latin scopus to Greek skopos, a target to aim at; Italian kept the aim, while English drifted to the room or range within which one acts.

scoppi.t: Sounds a little like a pop: scoppiare means to burst or explode, and a war or a quarrel scoppia when it breaks out.

scoppio.t: Sounds a little like a pop: scoppiare means to burst or explode, and a war or a quarrel scoppia when it breaks out.

scorre.t: From Latin excurrere: scorrere means to run or flow, as water or traffic does.

scorrevole.t: From scorrere (to slide, run or flow): scorrevole means sliding, moving or flowing freely.

scorrimento.t: From scorrere (to run or flow): scorrimento is flow, so a strada a scorrimento veloce is a road where traffic flows fast.

sede.t: Inherited from Latin sedes. Sede means a venue, a branch office or a seat, and it is also the word for a bishop's see.

sedile.t: From Latin sedile: a sedile is a seat, such as a seat in a vehicle, or a bench.

segatura.t: From segare (to saw): segatura is the dust that sawing leaves behind, sawdust.

seggiolino.t: From seggiola (chair) with the small ending -ino: a little seat, the child seat.

sella.t: From Latin sella, which shares an ancient root with sede (seat): a sella is a saddle, on a horse, a bicycle or a motorcycle.

selvatici.t: From Latin silvaticus, built on silva (forest), and related to the French sauvage: selvatico means wild or untamed, said of an animal or a plant.

semicarreggiata.t: From semi- (half) and carreggiata (roadway): one half of the roadway, the side used by one direction of traffic.

semirimorchi.t: From semi- (half) and rimorchio (trailer): a semi-trailer, which has no front axle and rests its front on the tractor.

semirimorchio.t: From semi- (half) and rimorchio (trailer): a semi-trailer, which has no front axle and rests its front on the tractor.

semovente.t: From se (itself) and movente (moving): moving by itself, that is, self-propelled.

sensibile.t: Not "sensible" in the sense of wise: sensibile means perceptible or noticeable, as in a change large enough to be sensed, and it can also mean sensitive. Both come from Late Latin sensibilis, perceptible by the senses; Italian kept that sense, while English "sensible" came to mean showing good sense.

senso.t: Besides "sense", senso often means direction, as in senso unico, one-way traffic.

serbatoi.t: From serbare (to keep), which comes from Latin servare: a serbatoio is a container where something is kept, such as a fuel tank.

serbatoio.t: From serbare (to keep), which comes from Latin servare: a serbatoio is a container where something is kept, such as a fuel tank.

servendosi.t: From servire (to serve): servirsi di means to make something serve oneself, that is, to use it.

servirsi.t: From servire (to serve): servirsi di means to make something serve oneself, that is, to use it.

servofreno.t: Built from servo and freno (brake): a servo brake, that is, a brake whose force is boosted, also called a power brake.

servosterzo.t: Built from servo and sterzo (steering): steering whose force is boosted, that is, power steering.

sfilamento.t: From sfilare, the opposite of infilare (to thread or slip on): sfilare is to slip something off or draw it out, as a thread from a needle.

sfilata.t: From sfilare, the opposite of infilare (to thread or slip on): sfilare is to slip something off or draw it out, as a thread from a needle.

sfiorano.t: Built on fiore (flower): its first sense was to strip away the flowers or the best part, and today sfiorare means to touch lightly, to graze or brush past.

sfondando.t: From s- (out) and fondo (bottom): to knock the bottom out of something, to break through it.

sfondare.t: From s- (out) and fondo (bottom): to knock the bottom out of something, to break through it.

sfregamenti.t: From Latin exfricare: sfregare means to rub or scrape, and sfregamenti are rubbings. The English "friction" likewise comes from a Latin word for a rubbing.

sfruttare.t: From frutto (fruit): sfruttare is to draw all the fruit out of something, to make full use of it or exploit it.

sganciamento.t: From s- (un-) and gancio (hook): sganciare is to unhook, to unhitch or unfasten.

sgrassarlo.t: From s- (removing) and grasso (fat, grease, related to the English "grease"): to remove the grease, to degrease.

sigillato.t: Related to sigillo (seal), from the Latin sigillum, the same word that gives the English "sigil", a seal or sign.

sintonizzare.t: From sintonia (being in tune), Greek syn (together) and tonos (tone): to bring the radio into the same tone as the station.

slitta.t: Linked to slitta (sled), a word related to the English "sled" and "slide": slittare is to slide or skid, losing grip.

slittamento.t: Linked to slitta (sled), a word related to the English "sled" and "slide": slittare is to slide or skid, losing grip.

slittare.t: Linked to slitta (sled), a word related to the English "sled" and "slide": slittare is to slide or skid, losing grip.

smontare.t: The opposite of montare (to mount, assemble): smontare is to take apart or remove, like the English "dismount".

smontata.t: The opposite of montare (to mount, assemble): smontare is to take apart or remove, like the English "dismount".

sobbalzano.t: Built on balzare (to leap, to bounce): sobbalzare is to give a sudden jump, to jolt.

soccorrere.t: From Latin succurrere (to run to help), the root of the English "succor": to come to the aid of someone.

solco.t: From Latin sulcus (furrow), a word anatomists still use in English for a groove.

solitamente.t: Not "solitarily": solitamente means usually or as a rule, built from solito and the adverb ending -mente. Solito comes from Latin solitus, past participle of solere (to be accustomed), while the English "solitary" comes from a different Latin word, solus (alone).

sollecitamente.t: In these statements sollecitamente means promptly, without delay, though it can also mean with attentive care, as "solicitously" does.

sollecitare.t: Besides "solicit", sollecitare means to urge or hurry someone, and said of a part or material, to put it under stress.

sollecitazioni.t: Here sollecitazioni are stresses, the forces acting on a part or material, rather than "solicitations", from sollecitare in its sense of to stress.

solleva.t: From Latin sublevare, sub (from below) and levare (to lift), as in the English "lever" and "elevate": to lift up.

sollevamento.t: From Latin sublevare, sub (from below) and levare (to lift), as in the English "lever" and "elevate": to lift up.

somministrargli.t: Related to the English "administer": both come from Latin ministrare (to serve, supply). Somministrare is to give a medicine or a drink.

sonnolenza.t: Related to the English "somnolent" (sleepy): both come from Latin somnus (sleep), the root of sonno.

sopraggiungano.t: From sopra (over, beyond) and giungere (to arrive): to arrive on the scene, as a vehicle that comes up or approaches.

sopravvalutare.t: From sopra (over) and valutare (to value, evaluate): to overvalue, to overestimate.

sordocieco.t: From sordo (deaf) and cieco (blind): deaf and blind at once.

sorgano.t: From Latin surgere (to rise), the root of the English "surge" and "insurgent": to rise or arise.

sorgono.t: From Latin surgere (to rise), the root of the English "surge" and "insurgent": to rise or arise.

sostare.t: From sostare, Latin substare (to stand still): a halt, here a vehicle left standing.

sostegni.t: From sostenere (to hold up, related to the English "sustain"): a support or stand.

sostenendo.t: Besides "sustain", sostenere means to hold up or to back, and with an exam as its object it means to take it, as in sostenere l'esame.

sostenere.t: Besides "sustain", sostenere means to hold up or to back, and with an exam as its object it means to take it, as in sostenere l'esame.

sottopassaggi.t: From sotto (under) and passaggio (passage): a passage that runs underneath, an underpass.

sottopassaggio.t: From sotto (under) and passaggio (passage): a passage that runs underneath, an underpass.

sottopassi.t: From sotto (under) and passaggio (passage): a passage that runs underneath, an underpass.

sottoporsi.t: From sotto (under) and porre (to put): sottoporsi is to put oneself under something, to undergo it, like the English "submit".

sottoposto.t: From sotto (under) and porre (to put): sottoporsi is to put oneself under something, to undergo it, like the English "submit".

sottostanti.t: The present participle of sottostare, from sotto (below) and stare: lying immediately underneath.

sottostimare.t: From sotto (under) and stimare (to estimate): to estimate too low, to underestimate.

sottovalutazione.t: From sottovalutare, sotto (under) and valutare (to value): the act of valuing something too low.

sottovia.t: From sotto (under) and via (way, road): a road that passes underneath, an underpass.

sottrazione.t: The Italian form of "subtraction", from Latin subtrahere (to draw away): a taking away or deduction.

sovraccarico.t: From sovra (over) and carico (load): an overload.

sovrannumero.t: Like soprannumero, from sopra or sovra (over) and numero (number): beyond the number that is set or permitted.

sovrapassaggi.t: From sovra (over) and passaggio (passage): a passage that runs overhead, an overpass.

sovrappassi.t: From sovra (over) and passaggio (passage): a passage that runs overhead, an overpass.

spargere.t: From Latin spargere (to scatter), the root of the English "sparse" and "disperse": to scatter or spill.

spargimento.t: From Latin spargere (to scatter), the root of the English "sparse" and "disperse": to scatter or spill.

spartitraffico.t: From spartire (to divide, share out) and traffico (traffic): the strip that divides the traffic, a median.

spaventarla.t: Spaventare goes back to Latin expavere (to take fright), and paura (fear) to pavor, from pavere (to be afraid). Spaventare is to frighten.

spaventarlo.t: Spaventare goes back to Latin expavere (to take fright), and paura (fear) to pavor, from pavere (to be afraid). Spaventare is to frighten.

spazzatura.t: From spazzare (to sweep): spazzatura is what is swept up, the garbage.

specchi.t: From Latin speculum (mirror), from specere (to look), as in the English "inspect".

specchietto.t: A small specchio (mirror), from Latin speculum, from specere (to look), as in the English "inspect".

specchio.t: From Latin speculum (mirror), from specere (to look), as in the English "inspect".

specie.t: Not "species" here: as an adverb, specie, alone or in in specie, means especially. The noun specie is Latin species, a kind, and English "special" and "especial" come from the related Latin specialis, belonging to a particular kind; so the adverb specie singles out one kind, just as "especially" does.

spessore.t: From spesso (thick, dense): spessore is how thick something is.

spetta.t: From Latin spectare (to look toward): spettare a means to be due to someone, to be their task.

spia.t: Besides a "spy", spia is a warning light, a signal on the dashboard that shows whether a part is working or has a fault.

sporgano.t: From Latin exporrigere, ex (out) and porrigere (to stretch out): sporgere is to stick out beyond an edge.

sporge.t: From Latin exporrigere, ex (out) and porrigere (to stretch out): sporgere is to stick out beyond an edge.

sporgono.t: From Latin exporrigere, ex (out) and porrigere (to stretch out): sporgere is to stick out beyond an edge.

sportello.t: Picture a small porta (door): a sportello is a small door, such as a car door or a service window.

sprovvisti.t: Provvisto (supplied) with the prefix s- that reverses it: sprovvisto means lacking, not supplied with.

squilibrata.t: Taken from equilibrare (to balance), with s- in place of the first e-: to throw out of balance.

stabilimenti.t: Related to the English "establishment", both going back to Latin stabilire: in these statements a stabilimento is a factory or industrial plant.

staccabatteria.t: Read it as stacca (detaches) and batteria (battery): the switch that detaches the battery.

staccare.t: The opposite of attaccare (to attach): staccare is to detach.

stagna.t: From stagnare, to coat or solder with tin (stagno), and then to seal every seam of a barrel or hull. A container a tenuta stagna lets no liquid in or out.

stalli.t: Related to the English "stall", as in the stalls of a barn: stalli are marked parking spaces, each for one vehicle, set side by side.

stampigliata.t: Related to stampa (print) and the English "stamp": stampigliare is to mark with a stamp.

statale.t: Not a US state: statale refers to the Italian State, the national government, so a strada statale is a national highway run by the State. It is built on stato, the political state, which comes from Latin status like English "state"; the English sense of one member of a federal union came later and is not what statale means.

stazionamento.t: Related to the English "stationary", both from Latin statio: stazionare means to stay parked or stand in one place, and stazionamento is that standing.

stazionare.t: Related to the English "stationary", both from Latin statio: stazionare means to stay parked or stand in one place, and stazionamento is that standing.

sterzare.t: Sounds a little like "steer": sterzare is to steer or swerve, and sterzo is the steering wheel.

sterzata.t: Sounds a little like "steer": sterzo is the steering wheel, and a sterzata is a turn of the wheel or a swerve.

sterzo.t: Sounds a little like "steer": sterzo is the steering wheel, and a sterzata is a turn of the wheel or a swerve.

stipulare.t: Not "stipulate" in the sense of setting a condition: stipulare means to draw up or conclude a contract, such as taking out an insurance policy. Both come from Latin stipulari, to bargain or exact a promise; English "stipulate" first meant to make a contract too, but that sense died out and it now means to demand a term as a condition.

stipulate.t: Not "stipulate" in the sense of setting a condition: stipulare means to draw up or conclude a contract, such as taking out an insurance policy. Both come from Latin stipulari, to bargain or exact a promise; English "stipulate" first meant to make a contract too, but that sense died out and it now means to demand a term as a condition.

stranieri.t: Straniero mainly means foreign, or a foreigner from another country, where the English "stranger" means someone you do not know.

strato.t: Related to the English "stratum" (plural strata): a layer.

strettoia.t: From stretto (narrow): a strettoia is a narrow spot where the road tightens.

stringere.t: Related to the English "stringent" and "constrict": all go back to the Latin stringere (to draw tight).

stringersi.t: Related to the English "stringent" and "constrict": all go back to the Latin stringere (to draw tight).

stringhe.t: Sounds like "string": a stringa is the string that ties a shoe, a shoelace.

strisciamento.t: From strisciare (to drag or crawl along a surface): the sliding of a tire across the road.

strisciano.t: Picture a snake: strisciare means to crawl or drag along the ground.

subisce.t: From the Latin subire, sub (under) and ire (to go): literally to under-go, exactly like the English "undergo".

subiscono.t: From the Latin subire, sub (under) and ire (to go): literally to under-go, exactly like the English "undergo".

subiti.t: From the Latin subire, sub (under) and ire (to go): literally to under-go, exactly like the English "undergo".

successivamente.t: Not "successfully": successivamente means afterward or later, from successivo (next). Both go back to Latin succedere, to come after; English "success" once meant simply an outcome and only later a good one, while Italian successivo kept the plain sense of what comes next.

successivo.t: Not "successful": successivo means next or following, like the English "successive". Both go back to Latin succedere, to come after; English "succeed" later added the sense of turning out well, and "successful" belongs to that sense, while successivo kept "coming after".

suolo.t: From the Latin solum (ground, bottom), which is also behind the English "sole" of a foot or shoe: suolo is the ground.

supera.t: From the Latin superare (to go over), built on super (above): to get over a line, a limit or another vehicle.

svincolo.t: From s- (un-) and vincolo (a tie or bond): the point where traffic is released from the main road.

svolge.t: From s- and volgere (to turn), from the Latin volvere, root of "revolve": svolgere is to unroll, so to carry out, and svolgersi is for an event to go on.

svuotarne.t: From s- and vuotare (to empty), which is built on vuoto (empty): svuotare is to make something empty.

taluni.t: From tale (such) and uno (one): taluni means certain ones, some but not all.

talvolta.t: From tal(e) (such) and volta (time): at such times, so sometimes.

tamburi.t: Related to the English "tambourine": a tamburo is a drum, and a drum brake takes its name from the shape.

tamponamenti.t: Related to tampone (a plug or pad), which comes from the French "tampon": a tamponamento is a crash into the back of another vehicle.

tamponare.t: Related to tampone (a plug or pad), which comes from the French "tampon": a tamponamento is a crash into the back of another vehicle.
