tamponati.t: Related to tampone (a plug or pad), which comes from the French "tampon": a tamponamento is a crash into the back of another vehicle.

tangenziale.t: As a noun, a tangenziale is a beltway or bypass, a fast road that runs around the edge of a city, not a "tangential" matter.

tappeti.t: Related to the English "tapestry": both go back to a Greek word for a rug or carpet.

tarare.t: Related to the English "tare", the weight of an empty container: tarare is to set or calibrate an instrument.

targa.t: Related to the English "target", which first meant a small shield: a targa is the flat plate that carries a vehicle's registration.

targhe.t: Related to the English "target", which first meant a small shield: a targa is the flat plate that carries a vehicle's registration.

targhetta.t: Diminutive of targa (plate), related to the English "target", which first meant a small shield: a small identifying plate or tag.

telaio.t: From tela (cloth): first the frame of a weaving loom, then any supporting frame, such as a chassis.

telo.t: From tela (cloth): a single piece of fabric used on its own, such as a towel, a tent panel or a cover.

telonati.t: From telone (a large tarp, from tela, cloth): covered with a tarp.

tempestivamente.t: Not "tempestuously": tempestivamente means in a timely way, promptly and at the right moment. Both go back to Latin tempestas, which first meant a time or season and only later a storm; tempestivo keeps the old sense of the right time, while English "tempestuous" comes from the storm.

temporizzati.t: Not "temporized" in the sense of stalling for time: temporizzati means set to run on a timer, from the Latin tempus (time). Italian built temporizzare on that root as a technical word for timing a device, while English "temporize" came from a French verb meaning to wait one's time, hence to stall.

tenditore.t: From tendere (to stretch, as in "tension"): the device that keeps something taut.

tenuto.t: From tenere (to hold): essere tenuto a is to be held to something, that is, obliged to do it.

tergicristallo.t: From tergere (to wipe, as in detergent) and cristallo (glass): the thing that wipes the glass.

terriccio.t: From terra (earth): the top layer of soil, mixed with the remains of leaves and other plant matter.

tessuti.t: From tessere (to weave), like the English "textile": tessuto is woven fabric, and the English "tissue" comes from the same weaving word.

tettuccio.t: Diminutive of tetto (roof): a small roof, used for the removable hard top of a convertible car.

titolare.t: From titolo (title): the titolare is the person in whose name something stands, the holder of a license or document.

tombini.t: A diminutive of tomba (tomb), like a little tomb: the stone or iron lid over a drain opening in the road.

tornante.t: From the French tournant, from tourner (to turn): a bend of nearly a half circle, where the road turns back on itself.

traforo.t: From tra- (through) and forare (to bore a hole, as in "perforate"): a tunnel bored through a mountain.

tragitti.t: From the Latin traiectus (a crossing), the same root as the English "trajectory": a tragitto is the route from one place to another.

traina.t: Related to the English "train": both come from the French verb for dragging, and trainare means to tow or haul something behind you.

trainando.t: Related to the English "train": both come from the French verb for dragging, and trainare means to tow or haul something behind you.

trainano.t: Related to the English "train": both come from the French verb for dragging, and trainare means to tow or haul something behind you.

trainante.t: Related to the English "train": both come from the French verb for dragging, and trainare means to tow or haul something behind you.

trainare.t: Related to the English "train": both come from the French verb for dragging, and trainare means to tow or haul something behind you.

trainati.t: Related to the English "train": both come from the French verb for dragging, and trainare means to tow or haul something behind you.

traini.t: Related to the English "train": both come from the French verb for dragging, and trainare means to tow or haul something behind you.

traino.t: Related to the English "train": both come from the French verb for dragging, and trainare means to tow or haul something behind you.

tramite.t: From the Latin trames (a path or byway): tramite means by way of or through.

tranne.t: From trarre (to draw out) and ne: literally take that out, so except.

trascorrano.t: From tra- (across) and correre (to run): time runs across, so it passes or elapses.

trascorsi.t: From tra- (across) and correre (to run): time runs across, so it passes or elapses.

trascurabile.t: From trascurare (to neglect), built on curare (to care for): small enough to be neglected, so negligible.

tratteggiate.t: From tratto (a stroke or short line): drawn in short strokes, so dashed.

trattenuti.t: From tra- and tenere (to hold): held back or restrained, like the English "retain", also built on the Latin tenere.

tratto.t: From trarre (to draw), like the English "tract": a stretch of road drawn from one point to another.

traversa.t: From traverso (crosswise), related to the English "traverse": a street that crosses the main one.

trombe.t: Related to the English "trumpet": a tromba is a trumpet, and also a vehicle's horn.

tutelare.t: Related to the English "tutelage" and "tutor": all come from the Latin tueri (to watch over, protect).

udito.t: From udire (to hear), related to the English "audio" and "audible".

ulteriori.t: Not "ulterior" in the sense of hidden: ulteriore means further or additional. Both come from Latin ulterior, farther or on the far side; English developed the sense of something beyond what is shown, as in an ulterior motive, while Italian uses the word for something added beyond what came before.

unicamente.t: Related to the English "uniquely", both from Latin unicus, only or single: unicamente means only or solely.

uniche.t: Related to the English "unique", both from Latin unicus, only or single: unico usually means the only one, as in senso unico, one-way traffic.

unico.t: Related to the English "unique", both from Latin unicus, only or single: unico usually means the only one, as in senso unico, one-way traffic.

urtare.t: Sounds a little like "hurt": urtare is to strike or bump into, and an urto is a knock or collision.

urto.t: Sounds a little like "hurt": urtare is to strike or bump into, and an urto is a knock or collision.

ustionato.t: Related to the Latin urere (to burn), which is also behind the English "combustion": an ustione is a burn.

ustioni.t: Related to the Latin urere (to burn), which is also behind the English "combustion": an ustione is a burn.

usufruire.t: Related to the English legal word "usufruct": both join the Latin usus (use) and fructus (fruit, benefit).

usura.t: Not "usury" here: in these statements usura means wear, the gradual damage from use, as on a tire. This usura was borrowed from French usure, from user, to use, so it is the mark that use leaves; the usura that means usury is a separate word from Latin usura, use, and both rest on the idea of using.

usurati.t: Not "usurious": here usurati means worn out, from usurare, the verb built on usura (wear). This usura came from French usure, from user, to use, so it is the wear that use leaves; English "usury" comes from Latin usura, payment for the use of money, so both words grow from the idea of use.

utente.t: From the Latin utens (using), related to the English "utility": an utente is a user.

vaganti.t: Related to the English "vagabond": both come from the Latin vagari (to wander).

vale.t: From valere (to be worth or to hold good), related to the English "valid" and "value".

valgono.t: From valere (to be worth or to hold good), related to the English "valid" and "value".

valicare.t: Related to valico, a mountain pass: valicare is to cross over a barrier, such as a line on the road.

vaschetta.t: From vasca (tub, basin) with the diminutive ending -etta: a small basin, here the reservoir that holds a fluid.

vedente.t: From vedere (to see): a vedente is a person who sees, so non vedente means blind.

velocipedi.t: Related to the English "velocipede", from the Latin velox (fast) and pes, pedis (foot): the legal word for a pedal cycle.

verificano.t: Not "verify" here: in the form verificarsi (si verifica) the verb means to occur or to happen, so si verifica un guasto means a fault occurs. English "verify" comes from Medieval Latin verificare, to make true; verificarsi also means to come true, and a thing that comes true is a thing that happens.

verificarsi.t: Not "verify" here: in the form verificarsi (si verifica) the verb means to occur or to happen, so si verifica un guasto means a fault occurs. English "verify" comes from Medieval Latin verificare, to make true; verificarsi also means to come true, and a thing that comes true is a thing that happens.

verificato.t: Not "verify" here: in the form verificarsi (si verifica) the verb means to occur or to happen, so si verifica un guasto means a fault occurs. English "verify" comes from Medieval Latin verificare, to make true; verificarsi also means to come true, and a thing that comes true is a thing that happens.

verifichino.t: Not "verify" here: in the form verificarsi (si verifica) the verb means to occur or to happen, so si verifica un guasto means a fault occurs. English "verify" comes from Medieval Latin verificare, to make true; verificarsi also means to come true, and a thing that comes true is a thing that happens.

vernici.t: Related to the English "varnish", which comes from the same medieval word; in Italian vernice means paint in general.

versarvi.t: From the Latin versare (to turn), the source of the English "versatile": to pour is to empty a container by tipping it. Versarvi means to pour onto it.

vetri.t: From the Latin vitrum (glass), the root of the English "vitreous": vetri are panes of glass, here the windows of a vehicle.

vettura.t: From the Latin vectura, built on vehere (to carry), the same verb behind the English "vehicle": a vettura is a car.

vieta.t: From the Latin vetare (to forbid), the source of the English "veto": vietare means to forbid, and vietato means forbidden.

vietare.t: From the Latin vetare (to forbid), the source of the English "veto": vietare means to forbid, and vietato means forbidden.

vietato.t: From the Latin vetare (to forbid), the source of the English "veto": vietare means to forbid, and vietato means forbidden.

vietino.t: From the Latin vetare (to forbid), the source of the English "veto": vietare means to forbid, and vietato means forbidden.

vige.t: From the Latin vigere (to be strong, to thrive), the root of "vigor": a rule that vige is in force.

vigenti.t: From the Latin vigere (to be strong, to thrive), the root of "vigor": a rule that vige is in force.

vigile.t: Not a "vigil": as a noun, vigile means a local police officer, such as one directing traffic. As an adjective it means vigilant or watchful. Both uses come from Latin vigil, awake or watchful, the root of the English "vigil" and "vigilant", so a vigile is a watchman.

vincolato.t: From vincolo (a bond or tie), from the Latin vinculum (bond, link): vincolato means bound or tied to something.

viscido.t: Not "viscous" (thick): viscido means slimy or slick, as a wet or greasy surface is. It comes from Latin viscidus, sticky, from viscum, the birdlime made from mistletoe, which is also the source of "viscous"; English kept the thick, slow-flowing side of that stickiness, while Italian kept the slimy, slippery side.

visita.t: Like the English "visit" in "a doctor's visit": in these statements a visita is a medical examination by a doctor.

viso.t: Related to the English "visage", both from the Latin visus (sight, appearance): viso means face.

visuale.t: Related to the English "visual", both from Late Latin visualis: as a noun, visuale is the view or line of sight a driver has.

visualizzare.t: Visualizzare mostly means to display or show something, or to view it, more often than "visualize".

vitalizio.t: Built on the Latin vitalis (vital): a vitalizio is an income paid for the rest of a person's life.

volante.t: Also the ordinary word for "flying", from volare (to fly); as a noun in a vehicle, volante is the steering wheel.

zebrature.t: From zebra: zebrature are painted stripes like a zebra's, the hatched white markings on the road surface.

ininfluente.t: Related to the English "influence": in- (not) plus influente (having influence), so without influence on the result, irrelevant. Both go back to the Latin influere, to flow in.

abitazioni.t: Related to the English "habitation": abitazione comes from the Latin habitatio and drops the h. It means a home or dwelling.

abituati.t: Related to the English "habituated": abituare comes from the Late Latin habituare and drops the h. Abituati means accustomed, used to something.

accordarsi.t: Related to the English "accord", as in "to reach an accord": accordarsi, the reflexive of accordare, means to come to an agreement with someone.

addome.t: Related to the English "abdomen": addome is borrowed from the Latin abdomen, with the "bd" turned into a double d.

aderente.t: Related to the English "adherent" and "adhesive": aderente, from aderire, describes something that sticks close to a surface, so snug or close-fitting.

alpinismo.t: Related to the English "Alps" and the rare "alpinism": alpinismo is mountaineering, a word linked to le Alpi, the Alps.

ambientale.t: Related to the English "ambient": ambientale comes from ambiente (environment), which goes back to the Latin ambiens, surrounding. So ambientale means environmental.

ambiente.t: Related to the English "ambient": both come from the Latin ambiens, surrounding. Ambiente is what surrounds you, the environment.

ammessi.t: Related to the English "admit": ammessi is the past participle of ammettere, from the Latin admittere, with the "dm" turned into a double m. It means admitted, allowed in.

ampiezza.t: Related to the English "ample": ampiezza comes from ampio (wide), from the Latin amplus, so it is wideness: width or breadth.

ampio.t: Related to the English "ample": ampio comes from the Latin amplus, with the "pl" turned into "pi". It means wide, broad or roomy.

ansia.t: Related to the English "anxiety" and "anxious": ansia comes from the Latin anxia, from anxius (anxious), with the x turned into s. It means anxiety.

anteriore.t: Related to the English "anterior": both come from the Latin anterior, from ante (before). Anteriore means front, the opposite of posteriore (rear).

anteriormente.t: Related to the English "anterior": anteriormente is the adverb of anteriore (front), from the Latin anterior, from ante (before). It means at the front.

apertura.t: Related to the English "aperture": apertura comes from the Latin apertura and is the everyday Italian word for an opening, the opposite of chiusura.

barrato.t: Related to the English "bar": barrare is to strike through with a bar (barra), so a barrato sign is one crossed out by a stripe, not "barred" in the sense of forbidden.

bilanciatura.t: Related to the English "balance": bilancia is a scale for weighing, and bilanciatura is the balancing. Both words go back to the Latin bilanx, a scale with two pans.

brusca.t: Related to the English "brusque", which English took through French from the Italian brusco. In Italian it describes a sudden, abrupt movement, not only a curt manner.

bruscamente.t: Related to the English "brusque", which English took through French from the Italian brusco. Bruscamente is its adverb: abruptly, suddenly.

brusche.t: Related to the English "brusque", which English took through French from the Italian brusco. In Italian it describes a sudden, abrupt movement, not only a curt manner.

busto.t: Related to the English "bust", which came through French from this Italian word for the upper body. An English bust is a sculpture of head and chest; busto is the torso itself.

cessano.t: Related to the English "cease" and "cessation": English took "cease" through French from the Latin cessare, the same form as the Italian verb.

commesse.t: Related to the English "commit": commesse is the feminine plural of commesso, the past participle of commettere, so violazioni commesse are violations committed. It is not the noun commessa, a shop assistant.

comportamento.t: Related to the English "comportment", the way a person conducts himself: comportamento is behavior. The English verb "comport" comes from the Latin comportare, built on portare, to carry.

concesso.t: Related to the English "concede" and "concession": concesso is the past participle of concedere, to grant or allow, so granted. Both go back to the Latin concedere.

concezione.t: Related to the English "conception" and "concept": concezione comes from the Latin conceptio. Here it means how a thing was conceived and planned, so its design.

confluenza.t: Related to the English "confluence", from the Latin for flowing together: con- (together) plus fluere (to flow). Here it is the point where one road flows into another, a merge.

contigui.t: Related to the English "contiguous": both come from the Latin contiguus, touching or bordering. Spaces that are contigui touch one another, so they are adjacent.

correnti.t: Related to the English "current": corrente comes from the Latin currentem, running, and the English word from the Latin currere, to run. Correnti di traffico are streams of moving traffic.

corso.t: Related to the English "course": corso comes from the Latin cursus and means course. In corso means in its course, so in progress or under way.

cosciente.t: Related to the English "conscious": cosciente comes from the Latin conscientem, and Italian dropped the n, so cons- became cos-. It means awake and aware.

decimi.t: Related to the English "decimal": both come from the Latin decimus, tenth. Decimi are tenths, the parts of a whole divided into ten.

decisamente.t: Related to the English "decisive": decisamente is deciso (decided, firm) plus the adverb ending -mente, so decisively or firmly. It can also mean definitely.

detriti.t: Related to the English "detritus": detrito comes from the Latin detritus. Detriti are loose broken fragments of rock and earth, that is, debris.

ecceda.t: Related to the English "exceed": Italian writes ecc where English has exc, as in eccesso and "excess". Both verbs come from the Latin excedere, to go beyond.

edifici.t: Related to the English "edifice", a large building: edificio, plural edifici, and "edifice" both come from the Latin aedificium, a building.

emesso.t: Related to the English "emit" and "emission": emesso is the past participle of emettere, to emit or issue. Both go back to the Latin emittere, to send out.

errata.t: Related to the English "err" and "error": errata is the feminine of errato, wrong or mistaken, from errare. English "err" comes from the Latin errare, to wander or go astray.

esaurito.t: Related to the English "exhaust": Italian writes es where English has ex, so esaurito means exhausted, used up. Both come from the Latin exhaurire, to draw off or use up.

esentato.t: Related to the English "exempt": esentare is esente (exempt) plus -are, and esente comes from the Latin exemptus, with the x turned to s and the mp dropped.

esercitata.t: Related to the English "exercise": esercitare comes from the Latin exercitare, and like "exercise" it can mean to exert a force or a power, so a force esercitata is a force exerted.

esercitare.t: Related to the English "exercise": esercitare comes from the Latin exercitare, and like "exercise" it can mean to exert a force or a power, so a force esercitata is a force exerted.

esibire.t: Related to the English "exhibit": esibire comes from the Latin exhibere, to hold out or show, with the h dropped and the x turned to s. To esibire a document is to show it when asked.

estetica.t: Related to the English "aesthetic", written the Italian way without the a. Estetico means having to do with looks rather than use, that is, cosmetic.

estintore.t: Related to the English "extinct" and "extinguish": estintore is borrowed from the Latin exstinctor, from the verb for putting out a fire, so it names the fire extinguisher.

estrarlo.t: Related to the English "extract": estrarre comes from the Latin extrahere, ex- (out) plus trahere (to pull), so it means to pull out. Estrarlo is estrarre plus lo, to pull it out.

estrarre.t: Related to the English "extract": estrarre comes from the Latin extrahere, ex- (out) plus trahere (to pull), so it means to pull out. Estrarlo is estrarre plus lo, to pull it out.

eventualità.t: Related to the English "eventuality", a possible event: eventualità means a possibility or a case that may arise, and nella sola eventualità che means only in the case that.

farmaci.t: Related to the English "pharmacy" and "pharmaceutical": farmaco comes from the Greek pharmakon, a drug, with the ph written as f. The farmacia is where farmaci are sold.

favorito.t: Related to the English "favor": favorire is formed from favore, and said of an event it means to help it along, so something favorito da a cause is made more likely by it.

favorire.t: Related to the English "favor": favorire is formed from favore, and said of an event it means to help it along, so something favorito da a cause is made more likely by it.

favorisce.t: Related to the English "favor": favorire is formed from favore, and said of an event it means to help it along, so something favorito da a cause is made more likely by it.

fiamme.t: Related to the English "flame": fiamma comes from the Latin flamma, and Italian turned its fl into fi. Fiamme is the plural, flames.

garze.t: Related to the English "gauze": garza is probably borrowed from the French gaze, a name tied to the city of Gaza. Garze sterili are sterile gauze pads.

idraulico.t: Related to the English "hydraulic": idraulico comes from the Latin hydraulicus, with the h dropped and the y written as i. As a noun, idraulico also means a plumber.

igienico.t: Related to the English "hygienic": igienico is formed from igiene, hygiene, spelled without the h and y. Servizi igienico-sanitari are bathroom facilities such as toilets and washbasins.

impartiti.t: Related to the English "impart": impartire comes from the Latin impartire, in- plus partire (to divide, share out). Ordini impartiti are orders given out, that is, issued.

impedire.t: Related to the English "impede", but stronger: impedire means to prevent, to stop something happening. It comes from the Latin impedire, formed on pes, pedis (foot), as if hobbling the feet.

impedisce.t: Related to the English "impede", but stronger: impedire means to prevent, to stop something happening. It comes from the Latin impedire, formed on pes, pedis (foot), as if hobbling the feet.

impedirgli.t: Related to the English "impede", but stronger: impedire means to prevent, to stop something happening. It comes from the Latin impedire, formed on pes, pedis (foot), as if hobbling the feet.

impedito.t: Related to the English "impede", but stronger: impedire means to prevent, to stop something happening. It comes from the Latin impedire, formed on pes, pedis (foot), as if hobbling the feet.

impediscano.t: Related to the English "impede", but stronger: impedire means to prevent, to stop something happening. It comes from the Latin impedire, formed on pes, pedis (foot), as if hobbling the feet.

incendi.t: Related to the English "incendiary", which describes something that starts fires. Both come from the Latin incendium, a fire; incendi is the plural of incendio.

incendio.t: Related to the English "incendiary", which describes something that starts fires. Both come from the Latin incendium, a fire, and an incendio is a fire or blaze.

incorre.t: Related to the English "incur": both come from the Latin incurrere, to run into. Incorrere in a penalty is to run into it, that is, to incur it.

incorrere.t: Related to the English "incur": both come from the Latin incurrere, to run into. Incorrere in a penalty is to run into it, that is, to incur it.

incosciente.t: Related to the English "conscious": in- (not) plus cosciente (conscious), so unconscious. Both go back to the Latin conscire, to be aware. The word can also mean reckless.

influisce.t: Related to the English "influence": both go back to the Latin influere, to flow in. Influire su something is to have an influence on it, to affect it.

influiscono.t: Related to the English "influence": both go back to the Latin influere, to flow in. Influire su something is to have an influence on it, to affect it.

iniettori.t: Related to the English "injector": Italian writes -iett- where English writes -ject-. Both go back to the Latin inicere, to throw in, and iniettare means to inject.

iscrizione.t: Related to the English "inscription": both come from the Latin inscriptio, and Italian dropped the n. The word also means enrollment or registration.

istituito.t: Related to the English "institute": both come from the Latin instituere, to set up, and Italian dropped the n, so istituito means set up or established.

leve.t: Related to the English "lever": leva comes from levare, to raise, and "lever" goes back through French to the Latin levare, so both name a bar used to lift or move something.

maggior.t: Related to the English "major": maggiore and "major" both come from the Latin maior, greater, so maggiore means greater or larger, and maggior is its short form.

maggiore.t: Related to the English "major": maggiore and "major" both come from the Latin maior, greater, so maggiore means greater or larger, and maggior is its short form.

maggiormente.t: Related to the English "major": maggiormente is maggiore (greater, from the Latin maior, like "major") plus -mente, so it means to a greater degree, more.

manovra.t: Related to the English "maneuver": both come through Old French from the Latin manu, by hand, and opera, work, so a manovra is a controlled movement, first of work done by hand.

manovrare.t: Related to the English "maneuver": both come through Old French from the Latin manu, by hand, and opera, work, so a manovra is a controlled movement, first of work done by hand.

mantenere.t: Related to the English "maintain": both come from the Latin manu tenere, to hold in the hand, and mantenere is plainly mano plus tenere, so it means to keep or hold.

mantenuta.t: Related to the English "maintain": both come from the Latin manu tenere, to hold in the hand, and mantenere is plainly mano plus tenere, so it means to keep or hold.

mantenendo.t: Related to the English "maintain": both come from the Latin manu tenere, to hold in the hand, and mantenere is plainly mano plus tenere, so it means to keep or hold.

mantenersi.t: Related to the English "maintain": both come from the Latin manu tenere, to hold in the hand, and mantenere is plainly mano plus tenere, so it means to keep or hold.

miopia.t: The same word as the English "myopia", nearsightedness, from the Greek myops, literally closing the eyes, since nearsighted people squint.

motoveicoli.t: Not any "motor vehicle": motoveicolo, from moto- and veicolo, names only the two- or three-wheeled class of motor vehicle, the one that includes motorcycles.

norma.t: Related to the English "norm": both come from the Latin norma, a rule or standard, so di norma means as a rule, normally.

normativa.t: Related to the English "norm" and "normative": a normativa, built on norma (rule), is the body of rules on a subject, its regulations.

notturne.t: Related to the English "nocturnal": notturno comes from the Latin nocturnus, from nox (night), the same source as Italian notte, so notturne means of the night.

nozioni.t: Related to the English "notion": both come from the Latin notio, from noscere (to know). In the plural, nozioni are the basic facts of a subject, its rudiments.

omesso.t: Related to the English "omit": omesso is the past participle of omettere, from the Latin omittere, so l'omesso uso is an omitted use, a failure to use.

omogenea.t: Related to the English "homogeneous", written without the h: omogeneo means the same throughout, so non omogenea means uneven.

operatrici.t: Related to the English "operator": operatrice is the feminine form of operatore, agreeing with macchina, so macchine operatrici are machines that do work.

ospedale.t: Related to the English "hospital": ospedale comes from the Late Latin hospitale, a shelter or guesthouse, with the h dropped and the t softened to d.

ostacola.t: Related to the English "obstacle": ostacolare is built on ostacolo (obstacle), from the Latin obstaculum, so it means to be an obstacle to, to hinder.

ostacolare.t: Related to the English "obstacle": ostacolare is built on ostacolo (obstacle), from the Latin obstaculum, so it means to be an obstacle to, to hinder.

ostacolarne.t: Related to the English "obstacle": ostacolare is built on ostacolo (obstacle), from the Latin obstaculum, so it means to be an obstacle to, to hinder.

ottimali.t: Related to the English "optimal": Italian writes tt where English has pt, as in ottimo (best), so condizioni ottimali are the best possible conditions.

ovalizzazione.t: Related to the English "oval": ovalizzazione comes from ovalizzare, to make oval, so it names a round shape wearing into an oval one.

pallida.t: Related to the English "pallid" and "pale": all come from the Latin pallidus (pale), so pallida simply means pale.

pericolosità.t: Built on pericoloso (dangerous), from pericolo (peril, danger), plus -ità, the ending of English "-ity" words, so pericolosità is dangerousness, how dangerous something is.

portici.t: Related to the English "portico", which was borrowed from this Italian word: portici are arcades, covered walkways along the front of buildings.

posteriore.t: Related to the English "posterior": both come from the Latin posterior, coming after. In Italian it is the everyday word for rear or back, as in the back of a vehicle.

posteriormente.t: Related to the English "posterior": posteriore (rear, from the Latin posterior) plus -mente, so at the rear or from behind.

potenza.t: Related to the English "potent" and "potency": both come from the Latin potentia, power. For an engine or motor, potenza is its power output.

praticabile.t: Related to the English "practicable", which also comes from the verb meaning to practice. Of a road or shoulder, praticabile means usable, fit to be driven or walked on.

praticati.t: Related to the English "practice": praticare means to put into practice, and with treatments or first aid it means to perform or carry out. Both go back to the Greek prassein, to do.

preannuncia.t: Related to the English "announce": pre- (before) plus annunciare (to announce), so to announce in advance, to give warning of something ahead.

preannunciare.t: Related to the English "announce": pre- (before) plus annunciare (to announce), so to announce in advance, to give warning of something ahead.

preannunciate.t: Related to the English "announce": pre- (before) plus annunciare (to announce), so to announce in advance, to give warning of something ahead.

precedenza.t: Related to the English "precedence": from precedere (to go before) plus -enza. Having precedenza means the right to go first, the right of way.

precluso.t: Related to the English "preclude": both come from the Latin praecludere, to close off in front, from prae (before) and claudere (to shut). Precluso means blocked or prevented.

premio.t: Related to the English "premium": both come from the Latin praemium, reward. English took the insurance sense from Italian premio, which also means a prize.

presenta.t: Related to the English "present" in the sense to show. Said of a thing, presentare often means that it has or shows a feature, as a road presenting a hazard.

presentano.t: Related to the English "present" in the sense to show. Said of a thing, presentare often means that it has or shows a feature, as a road presenting a hazard.

presentare.t: Related to the English "present" in the sense to show. Said of a thing, presentare often means that it has or shows a feature, as a road presenting a hazard.

profonda.t: Related to the English "profound": both come from the Latin profundus, deep. English uses profound mostly figuratively, while Italian profondo is the everyday word for deep.

propagarsi.t: Related to the English "propagate": both come from the Latin propagare, to extend or spread. Propagarsi is to spread, as flames spread along a line of vehicles.

proprietario.t: Related to the English "proprietor": both go back to the Medieval Latin proprietarius, of a property owner. The proprietario is the owner.

prossimità.t: Related to the English "proximity": both come from the Latin proximitas. Italian writes ss where English has x, so in prossimità di means near.

provvisoria.t: Related to the English "provisional": both go back to the Latin providere, to provide for. Provvisorio means temporary, arranged for now and meant to be replaced.

pubblicitaria.t: Related to the English "publicity": in Italian pubblicità is the usual word for advertising, so pubblicitario means advertising, as in an advertising sign.

ridotta.t: Related to the English "reduce": ridotta is the feminine past participle of ridurre, which comes from the Latin reducere, to reduce. So ridotta means reduced.

rifrangente.t: Related to the English "refract": rifrangente comes from rifrangere, to refract or break again, from the Latin refringere, to break up. Both words describe light sent back or bent.

rimosso.t: Related to the English "remove": rimosso is the past participle of rimuovere, from the Latin removere, re- plus movere, to move. So rimosso means removed.

riprodotto.t: Related to the English "reproduce": riprodotto is the past participle of riprodurre, which is ri- plus produrre, to produce. So riprodotto means reproduced, here shown in a figure.

rispetto.t: Related to the English "respect", as in "with respect to": rispetto a means with respect to or in relation to something else. Rispetto comes from the Latin respectus.

rotatoria.t: Related to the English "rotary": the adjective rotatorio means rotating or rotary, from the Latin roto, and the noun rotatoria is a rotary, a roundabout or traffic circle.

rovinare.t: Related to the English "ruin": rovinare comes from the Latin ruinare, to ruin, and is built on rovina, a ruin.

rovinando.t: Related to the English "ruin": rovinare comes from the Latin ruinare, to ruin, and is built on rovina, a ruin.

rovinata.t: Related to the English "ruin": rovinare comes from the Latin ruinare, to ruin, and is built on rovina, a ruin.

schema.t: Related to the English "schema": here schema means a layout or diagram, as in a "schematic" drawing. It comes through Latin from the Greek skhema, form or shape.

soffocandole.t: Related to the English "suffocate": soffocare comes from the Latin suffocare, whose su- became so- in Italian. Soffocandole means smothering them, cutting off their air.

soggetto.t: Related to the English "subject": soggetto comes from the Latin subiectus, whose sub- became sog- in Italian. Soggetto a means subject to, exposed to.

sonori.t: Related to the English "sonorous": sonoro comes from the Latin sonorus and means producing sound, so segnali sonori are sound signals.

sospesa.t: Related to the English "suspended": sospesa is the past participle of sospendere, from the Latin suspendere, whose su- became so- in Italian.

sostituire.t: Related to the English "substitute": sostituire comes from the Latin substituere, whose subst- became sost- in Italian. It means to put one thing in place of another, to replace.

sostituito.t: Related to the English "substitute": sostituire comes from the Latin substituere, whose subst- became sost- in Italian. It means to put one thing in place of another, to replace.

sostituirle.t: Related to the English "substitute": sostituire comes from the Latin substituere, whose subst- became sost- in Italian. It means to put one thing in place of another, to replace.

sostituisce.t: Related to the English "substitute": sostituire comes from the Latin substituere, whose subst- became sost- in Italian. It means to put one thing in place of another, to replace.

sostituiscono.t: Related to the English "substitute": sostituire comes from the Latin substituere, whose subst- became sost- in Italian. It means to put one thing in place of another, to replace.

sostituzione.t: Related to the English "substitution": sostituzione comes from the Latin substitutionem, whose subst- became sost- in Italian. It is the replacing of one thing with another.

stabilito.t: Related to the English "establish": both come from the Latin stabilire, to make stable, and English added an e- in front. Stabilito means established or set.

stabilire.t: Related to the English "establish": both come from the Latin stabilire, to make stable, and English added an e- in front. Stabilito means established or set.

strumenti.t: Related to the English "instrument": strumento comes from the older Italian instrumento, from the Latin instrumentum, and later dropped its in-. Strumenti are devices or tools.

suddivisa.t: Related to the English "subdivided": suddividere comes from the Latin subdividere, whose subd- became sudd- in Italian. Suddivisa means divided into parts.

torace.t: Related to the English "thorax": torace comes from the Latin thorax, with th- written as t- in Italian. Torace is the ordinary Italian word for the chest.

uniformandola.t: Related to the English "uniform": uniformare, from uni- and formare, means to make uniform or to conform, so here uniformandola is matching it to something else.

valutabile.t: Related to the English "evaluate": valutare is built on valuta, from valere (to be worth), the Latin source of "evaluate" too, so to work out what something is worth, to judge.

valutare.t: Related to the English "evaluate": valutare is built on valuta, from valere (to be worth), the Latin source of "evaluate" too, so to work out what something is worth, to judge.

valutazione.t: Related to the English "evaluate": valutare is built on valuta, from valere (to be worth), the Latin source of "evaluate" too, so to work out what something is worth, to judge.

regolazione.t: Besides regulation, it means adjustment, the setting of a device such as a mirror or a seat. English regulate once had the same sense, to adjust a clock, and both come from Latin regula, a straight bar or rule.

giunti.t: Past participle of giungere, to arrive, which comes from Latin iungere, to join. Giunti in prossimità means having arrived near. It is not giuntare, which means to join two pieces together, as with tape or thread.
